name: Aipan
tagline: White rice-paste patterns drawn by hand on red earth floors and walls, for every Kumaoni ritual.
facts: Form: ritual floor and wall painting
Materials: red geru earth and white rice paste (bisvar)
Made mostly by women, taught from mother to daughter
Received a GI certificate, dated to September 2021 by Wikipedia
art: Aipan is the ritual folk art of Kumaon. The name is linked to the Sanskrit word lepana, meaning plaster. Designs are drawn on house floors, walls, and the wooden stools and boards used in worship.

The base is geru, a red mud that is spread on the surface. The white lines are drawn over it with bisvar, a paste made by grinding rice in water. Women usually draw with their fingers. Many households today also use red and white enamel or acrylic paints.

Outlook Traveller says each design begins and ends with a central dot, which stands for the core of the universe, and the other lines radiate from it. Motifs include flowers, geometric patterns, conch shells, swastikas and the footprints of goddesses.

Designs are named for the ritual they serve. Sources list the Saraswati chowki for learning, the Nav Durga chowki for Devi worship, the Chamunda Hast chowki for havans, the Janeyu chowki for the sacred thread ceremony, and the Lakshmi yantra. They appear at festivals such as Makar Sankranti, Maha Shivaratri and Lakshmi Pujan, and at household ceremonies.
artist: Aipan belongs to the women of Kumaon. The skill passes from mothers to daughters and daughters-in-law, and is learned by watching and doing, not from a written manual.

Wikipedia names Minakshi Khati, who started the Minakriti Aipan Project in December 2019 to give rural Kumaoni women work and orders. The same article mentions a student project at a Delhi college that teaches Aipan artists business skills. I could not check these claims against a second source.
The sources I read do not name older individual artists, so none are named here.
place: Aipan comes from Kumaon, the eastern hill division of Uttarakhand. Wikipedia and Outlook Traveller both say it is believed to have started in Almora and flourished under the Chand dynasty, which ruled Kumaon from about the 15th century. This is a tradition and I found no firm documentation.

Outlook Traveller says migration carried the practice to other parts of the region, and that only some villages in Kumaon still keep it up as a daily household practice. The materials are local: red earth for the base and rice from the farm.

history.what: Aipan is said to have begun in Almora and to have flourished under the Chand rulers of Kumaon. No dated source was found.
Women carried the art as they moved, and it spread across Kumaon from floors and walls to household objects and cloth.
Wikipedia says the Uttarakhand government decided to acquire Aipan art for government buildings.
The Minakriti Aipan Project was launched by Minakshi Khati, according to Wikipedia.
Wikipedia says Aipan received a Geographical Indication certificate. Other web pages give a different year, so check the GI registry.

future: Training: workshops where older women teach the ritual meaning of each chowki to younger people, alongside the drawing skill.
Livelihood: orders for cloth, paper, wall panels and government buildings that pay women fairly for their time.
Materials: keep geru and rice paste in use at home and in ritual, with enamel and acrylic kept for objects that must last.
Documentation: record every named design with its occasion and the women who draw it, in Kumaoni and in English.
Protection: use the GI to keep the name for work from Kumaon and to tell buyers who made it.

name: Ajanta and Ellora
tagline: Two cave sites in one landscape: painted Buddhist halls and a temple carved from a hillside.
facts: Both are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, inscribed in 1983
Ajanta: 30 rock-cut Buddhist caves with wall paintings
Ellora: over 100 caves, 34 open to the public, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain
Kailasa temple (Cave 16) is attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I
art: Ajanta is a set of 30 rock-cut Buddhist caves cut into the side of a horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghora river. Many hold wall paintings. Wikipedia describes them as painted on dry plaster, and says the paintings are dimly lit and fragile.

The caves are usually described in two phases. The first is dated from the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE. The second is traditionally dated to about 400 to 650 CE. The scholar Walter Spink argued that most of the second phase was done in a short period of 460 to 480 CE under the Vakataka emperor Harishena. Other scholars argue for a longer timeline, and the Archaeological Survey of India still uses the traditional dating.

Ellora is a separate site, some distance to the south-west. Wikipedia counts over 100 caves cut into basalt cliffs, of which 34 are open to visitors: 12 Buddhist (caves 1 to 12), 17 Hindu (13 to 29) and 5 Jain (30 to 34). Its work is dated to about 600 to 1000 CE, and the dates of the Hindu caves are debated.

The best-known cave at Ellora is Cave 16, the Kailasa temple, dedicated to Shiva and carved out of a single rock. Wikipedia gives a courtyard of about 82 by 46 metres and a height of about 30 metres, and attributes it to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the later 8th century. Ellora is best known for sculpture, while Ajanta is best known for painting.
artist: Nobody can name the painters or carvers of Ajanta with certainty. The work was done by teams of masons, sculptors and painters, paid by kings, ministers and monks. Spink's reading ties the second phase to the court of Harishena, but this is one scholar's argument.

At Ellora the patrons shifted with the centuries. The early Buddhist caves are followed by the Hindu caves, mostly linked to the Rashtrakutas, and then the Jain caves, some of which Wikipedia associates with the Yadava period. The Kailasa attribution to Krishna I rests partly on a later copper plate; scholars cited by Wikipedia treat the attribution as accepted but not certain.
Today the people who hold the sites are conservators, guides and local families. In the early 1920s, Wikipedia says, the last Nizam of Hyderabad had the paintings restored by Italian experts.
place: Both sites are in Aurangabad district, on the Deccan plateau. Ajanta sits above the Waghora river gorge. Ellora is about 29 km north-west of Aurangabad, carved into the Charanandri hills.

Ajanta was hidden in jungle for centuries. Wikipedia reports that a British officer, John Smith, came across it on 28 April 1819 while hunting tigers, though local people already knew of it. The ASI protects both sites today.
Crowds are now the main pressure. Wikipedia reports that in 2012 replicas of caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 were planned at the Ajanta visitor centre to reduce crowding in the originals.

history.what: First phase of cave-cutting at Ajanta, probably under the Satavahanas according to Spink.
Second phase at Ajanta. Scholars differ on how long it lasted.
Buddhist phase at Ellora, per scholars cited on Wikipedia.
Hindu and Jain phase at Ellora, including the Kailasa temple attributed to Krishna I.
Yadava period, to which some Jain caves are attributed.
John Smith's party rediscovers Ajanta.
The Nizam of Hyderabad has the Ajanta paintings restored and makes the site a museum.
Both Ajanta and Ellora are inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

future: Training: support conservators, restorers and guides from the local area, with long-term jobs.
Livelihood: spread tourism income to nearby villages, craft workers and small traders.
Materials: continue careful, minimal-intervention conservation of the paintings and the damp-prone rock.
Documentation: complete high-resolution records of every cave and publish them openly.
Protection: manage visitor numbers, as replicas and timed entry help to do.

name: Baiga Tattoo Art
tagline: Godna, the tattoos that mark a Baiga woman's life, now also drawn on paper.
facts: Name: godna
Community: Baiga
Practitioners: women only
Motifs: mountains, sun, dots, crosses, lines
art: Godna is the tattooing tradition of the Baiga. Village Square says the meanings were held in memory and on skin, and never written down. The art is fading.
Art Monthly says designs are mostly from nature. Triangular lines stand for mountains and a circle often for the sun. Symmetrical lines of varying thickness, dots and crosses also recur.

Tattoos are placed on the forehead, arms, legs, back, neck and elsewhere, and each placement marks a life stage. A forehead tattoo is made around puberty, and arm and leg tattoos are done by marriageable age (Art Monthly). Village Square names a forehead 'stove' motif as marking a girl's passage into womanhood.
Art Monthly says the tattoos are linked with beauty, healing and history, and are believed to continue into the afterlife as the ink becomes part of the body.
artist: Mangala Bai Maravi is a Baiga artist from Lalpur in Dindori district. Art Monthly says she is the daughter of Shanti Bai Maravi, a well-known tattoo artist, and learned from her mother.

Mangala now translates the designs onto paper and canvas. Earlier the designs were passed on orally or recreated from memory. Her work has brought her family a steady income, and her 2024 works were shown at the 24th Biennale of Sydney.
Village Square says Shanti Bai taught the Delhi tattoo artist Amit Arjel-Sharma, who documents the practice. Art Monthly says only women can carry the tradition forward.
place: Baiga live mainly in Madhya Pradesh. Wikipedia says the 2011 census counted 552,495 Baiga, with 414,526 in Madhya Pradesh, and the largest concentration in Mandla and Balaghat. Lalpur, in Dindori district, is the home of the artist Mangala Bai Maravi.
Wikipedia says the Baiga traditionally avoid ploughing, as they believe it harms the Earth, and practise shifting cultivation known as bewar.

history.what: I found no dated source for the beginning of Baiga godna.
Women tattoo girls at set stages from puberty to marriage (Art Monthly).
Village Square says the art is fading and its meanings are no longer being passed on.
Amit Arjel-Sharma finds a Baiga village by online search to learn godna (Village Square).
Mangala Bai Maravi's work is shown at the 24th Biennale of Sydney (Art Monthly).

future: Training: apprenticeships with senior tattooists, as in Shanti Bai's teaching.
Livelihood: paying work on paper and canvas lets families value the designs.
Materials: record the traditional needles and inks, which my sources do not describe.
Documentation: write down motif meanings with the women who know them, with their consent.
Protection: credit Baiga artists and respect the meaning of marks on skin when designs are copied.

name: Bhil Painting
tagline: Dotted animals and gods from the Bhil wall tradition of Jhabua, now also on paper and canvas.
facts: Community: Bhil, largest tribal group in India (Wikipedia)
Wall form: Pithora, in Jhabua region
Known for multi-coloured dots
Best-known painter: Bhuri Bai, Padma Shri 2021
art: Bhil painting is the art of the Bhil community of western Madhya Pradesh. Its wall form is Pithora, a ritual painting from the Jhabua region that is central to the Bhil religious and cultural life, according to The Better India.

The wall is first coated with cow dung, water and lime in a step called lipai. Colours were traditionally taken from flowers, leaves and spices. The Better India says the paintings show the sun, moon and horses, which are lucky motifs, and also daily life such as hunting, ploughing and farming, along with birds, animals and trees.

Wikipedia says the art is considered by some to be the oldest of India's tribal art forms, and resembles Australian Aboriginal art in its use of multi-coloured dots. This is a comparison, not a claim of connection.
Pithora was traditionally painted by men, per the sources. In recent decades Bhil artists have also worked on paper and canvas with acrylics.
artist: Bhuri Bai was born in Pitol village in Jhabua district. Wikipedia says she came to Bhopal and worked as a labourer at Bharat Bhavan, earning Rs 6 a day. There the artist Jagdish Swaminathan encouraged her to paint on paper. She was the first artist of her community to paint on paper.

The Better India says her community opposed her work because women were not expected to be artists, and that her husband later accepted it. Her honours, per Wikipedia, are the Shikhar Samman (1986), Ahalya Samman (1998), Rani Durgavati Award (2009) and Padma Shri (2021).

Her canvases show myth, village scenes and people with animals. Wikipedia says later works include modern things such as aeroplanes and mobile phones. Her work has been shown in India, the UK and the USA, per The Better India. The Better India says she worked at the Madhya Pradesh Tribal Museum in Bhopal, teaching and refining her techniques.
place: Jhabua district lies on the Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat border, between the Mahi river to the north and the Narmada to the south (The Better India). It is the home of the Bhil community, who historically depended on forests and later on farming.
Bhopal is where Bhil artists have found markets and institutions. Bharat Bhavan and the Tribal Museum are named in the sources as places where Bhuri Bai worked.

history.what: Bhil art is considered by some to be very old; I found no firm dates.
Pithora wall paintings are made for household ritual, mostly by men (sources I read).
Jagdish Swaminathan asks Bhuri Bai to paint on paper at Bharat Bhavan (The Better India).
Bhuri Bai receives the Shikhar Samman from the Government of Madhya Pradesh.
She receives the Ahalya Samman and the Rani Durgavati Award (Wikipedia).
Bhuri Bai receives the Padma Shri.

future: Training: teaching young Bhils, and girls in particular, in museums and village workshops.
Livelihood: fair sales through museum shops and exhibitions, so painting pays as a profession.
Materials: keep knowledge of natural colours and lipai walls alongside acrylic work.
Documentation: record the Pithora stories and rites with the priests who know them.
Protection: credit Bhil artists by name when their designs are used in products.

name: Bhimbetka Rock Art
tagline: Hunters, dancers and animals painted in rock shelters, some thousands of years old.
facts: Location: Raisen district, about 45 km from Bhopal
Shelters: over 750 in seven hills, about 400 with paintings
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003
Earliest paintings commonly dated to about 10,000 BCE
art: Bhimbetka is a group of rock shelters in the Vindhya foothills with one of the largest bodies of prehistoric painting in India. Wikipedia says the site has seven hills and over 750 shelters spread over about 10 km, and around 400 of them have paintings.

The themes are animals, hunts with spears and bows, communal dances, musical instruments, birds, and pregnant women and children. Later paintings show riders on horses, archers and religious signs. A rock popularly called Zoo Rock shows elephants, barasingha, bison and deer.

The colours are red, white and yellow, and in later paintings black from manganese oxide, red from hematite, and charcoal. Early paintings used vegetable colours, which have lasted partly because they were placed deep in niches.

Dating is not settled. The earliest paintings are commonly placed around 10,000 BCE, in the Mesolithic. V. S. Wakankar dated the earliest to the Upper Palaeolithic, possibly up to 40,000 years ago. Some popular sources repeat very early dates which I could not confirm from UNESCO text.
artist: The painters are unknown. They were hunter-gatherer people who lived in the shelters and later groups who used them. Some shelters were lived in for more than 100,000 years, according to Wikipedia. That is a statement about the site, not about the paintings.

The archaeologist V. S. Wakankar was the first to recognise their prehistoric importance. He reported several prehistoric rock shelters in 1957. The full scale of the site was understood only in the 1970s.
Nobody can speak for the painters. I have not named any group as their descendants, as I found no source that supports this.
place: Bhimbetka lies in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, about 45 km south-east of Bhopal, among sandstone hills and forest. The shelters are formed of large quartzite rocks.

The Bhimbetka group has 243 of the painted shelters and the nearby Lakha Juar group 178, according to Wikipedia. The largest shelter, called Auditorium cave, has a boulder nicknamed Chief's Rock or King's Rock. Wikipedia notes that there is no evidence of such a role.

The site is a protected monument of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) and has been under its care since 1990. UNESCO inscribed it in 2003 under criteria (iii) and (v). Pins here are approximate.

history.what: Some shelters were first lived in, per Wikipedia.
The earliest paintings, commonly placed in the Mesolithic. Wakankar argued for Upper Palaeolithic dates, which remain debated.
Paintings of riders, archers and religious signs are added over many centuries.
V. S. Wakankar reports several prehistoric shelters.
The full extent of the site is recognised.
The site is protected under Indian law and managed by the ASI.
UNESCO inscribes it as a World Heritage Site.

future: Training: guides from nearby villages can be trained in site care and interpretation.
Livelihood: visitor income is a real source of work for local people, if carefully managed.
Materials: paintings are on open rock and damaged by water, plants, smoke and touch. Conservation needs skilled hands.
Documentation: digital recording and a clear published list of shelters with dating methods would settle some debates.
Protection: ASI care and the World Heritage status protect the site. Visitors should keep to paths and never touch the paintings.

name: Cheriyal Scrolls
tagline: A story you unroll, painted on a bright red ground.
facts: Medium: cloth scroll
Look: vivid red background, comic-strip panels
Subject: Puranas, Ramayana, community histories
art: Cheriyal scrolls are long painted cloths, often several metres, arranged in rows of panels read like a picture book. The red background is distinctive and the figures are bold and lively.
They were made to accompany storytellers, who unrolled the scroll and narrated the tale scene by scene.
artist: Scroll painters are from the nakash community in Cheriyal and are linked to a community of bard-storytellers, the Kaki Padagollu, who commissioned and performed from the scrolls.
Today a small number of families keep the craft alive, now also making masks and toys, and the art has moved into galleries.
Our approach: record a performance with each scroll.
place: Cheriyal is a village in Telangana's Siddipet district in the Deccan plateau.
The region's villages once hosted travelling storytellers for communities that supported them.

history.what: Narrative scrolls were made for itinerant storytellers.
Demand from patron communities fell and the craft was near extinction.
Revived through craft bodies and sold to collectors and for home decor.

future: Support the families so more young painters take up the scroll.
Make a digital library with recorded narrations.
Revive the performing side with community partnerships.

images.alt: A Cheriyal scroll painting with rows of story panels on a red ground.
images.author: Subha murugan

name: Chitrakathi
tagline: Picture storytelling from Pinguli, where a bundle of painted sheets becomes a tale.
facts: Form: painted picture stories told with song
A bundle of 30 to 50 or more sheets is called a pothi
Pinguli, Sindhudurg, is the best-known centre
Parshuram Gangavane received the Padma Shri in 2021
art: Chitrakathi means picture story. Wikipedia describes it as a storytelling art in which a performer travels and narrates stories while showing painted pictures. Each story is on separate sheets kept together as a bundle called a pothi, which Wikipedia says has 30 to 50 pages and Google Arts and Culture says more than 50.

The subjects are mostly the Ramayana and Mahabharata and other mythological tales. Google Arts and Culture says natural colours were used on handmade paper, and that artists set the songs first and then painted pictures to support the performance. Wikipedia says the colours are brownish and stone based and the figures are stylised.

The tradition also includes puppets. Wikipedia lists leather shadow puppets and stringed wooden puppets alongside picture stories, though only the picture form is now called Chitrakathi. Parshuram Gangavane's family works in all three.
artist: The best-known living figure is Parshuram Gangavane of Pinguli village in Kudal taluka, Sindhudurg. Wikipedia says he belongs to the Thakar tribal community and learned Chitrakathi, string puppetry and leather shadow puppetry from his father and grandfather.

He began reviving the art in the 1970s, when he saw it near extinction. He turned part of the family cowshed into a museum and gallery, the Thakar Adivasi Kala Aangan, which holds old paintings, puppets and instruments. His sons Chetan and Eknath perform and help run it. He received the Padma Shri in January 2021.
A popular family tradition says the ancestors worked as spies for Shivaji, with travelling shows as cover. Wikipedia reports it as what the family says. We found no independent historical source.
place: Pinguli is a village in Kudal taluka of Sindhudurg district, in the Konkan. Google Arts and Culture also names Gawdewada in Sindhudurg for Chitrakathi wall paintings. The page says the art developed in the Maharashtra and Karnataka region.

The art survives mainly where families keep it. Wikipedia describes Chitrakathi as nearly extinct and warns that without support the storytelling could vanish within roughly 15 years, a claim we could not check.

history.what: Chitrakathi developed in the Maharashtra-Karnataka region as small painted images of religious and historical events, per Google Arts and Culture.
Families say their ancestors served as spies of Shivaji, with performance as cover. Not independently confirmed.
Parshuram Gangavane starts reviving the art.
Gangavane is awarded the Padma Shri.

future: Training: family workshops that teach painting, singing and puppet-making together.
Livelihood: bookings in schools, museums and festivals, and fair pay for the pothis.
Materials: handmade paper and natural colours made available at fair cost.
Documentation: record the songs and the full cycles of each pothi.
Protection: support the museum, and credit the Thakar families as owners of the tradition.

name: Godna Tattoo Art
tagline: Soot-ink tattoos worn as identity, from the Ram name of the Ramnamis to Baiga women's life marks.
facts: Godna is the word for tattooing in Chhattisgarh and nearby regions
Ramnami tattoos carry the name of Ram, up to the whole body
Baiga women are tattooed by Badnins from the Ojha community
Ink: soot from an oil lamp or burned kerosene
art: Godna is traditional tattooing. In Chhattisgarh and neighbouring regions it is practised by different communities, for different reasons. We follow two of them here, and the sources do not cover every community.

The Ramnami Samaj, a community in the Janjgir-Champa area, tattoo the name of Ram on the body. According to Sahapedia, they write it as a doubled Ram Ram, standing for the formless (nirgun) god and not for the Ram of the epic. Some Ramnamis are marked all over the body, including the eyelids. Sahapedia describes a ranking by extent: nakhshikh (whole body), shiromani (forehead) and badan (face). Others keep the faith without tattoos.

Baiga women's godna, as described by Sahapedia, follows life stages. The forehead comes first, around age 8 to 10. Back, arms and legs are done by marriageable age, thighs after marriage, and neck and breast after childbearing. Motifs include the cow's eye, triangular lines for mountains, a sun at the centre of the chest, and dots, crosses and circles. A moon shape on the forehead marks a Baiga woman. Village Square adds fire, crops, peacocks, fish and flowers.

For both, the ink is soot. A Ramnami source describes burning kerosene in a lamp under an earthen pot and scraping soot from the pot, then storing it in a coconut shell. Baiga Badnins use soot from a sesame-oil lamp mixed with water. They draw with a thin stick and prick the ink in with needles, one for thin lines and three or four tied together for thick ones (Sahapedia).
artist: Among the Baiga the tattooists are women called Badnins, of the Ojha community. Sahapedia says they learned from their mothers and grandmothers and work from memory. Village Square profiles Mangala Bai Marawi, a Badnin of Dindori in Madhya Pradesh who did her first tattoo at seven. She fears the art may fade within about a decade, and she is teaching a niece and drawing the designs on canvas and charts.
Among the Ramnamis, Sahapedia says designated members of the community apply the tattoo with wooden needles, often in childhood or before marriage.

Godna is not the same everywhere. A tattoo can be devotion, beauty, protection, or a marker of identity, and tales about its origin, such as one about Parvati told among the Gond, are stories and not documented history.
place: The Ramnami movement is traditionally linked to Charpara village in Janjgir-Champa district. Sahapedia calls its account of the founder, Parasuram, a popular legend. It says the movement is more than a century old and records that the samaj was recognised as an organisation in 1960. It holds a gathering called the Bada Bhajan Mela.

Baiga communities live in Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. Sahapedia says the fully tattooed women it met were mostly older women in interior villages of Dindori district in Madhya Pradesh, so we use these accounts for the wider Baiga tradition, not for Chhattisgarh alone.

history.what: No hard facts date the origin of godna, according to Homegrown. It is tied to myths.
Sahapedia reports that the Ramnami founder was born in Charpara in this period, and calls the tale a popular legend.
Sahapedia says the movement is more than a century old and its Bada Bhajan Mela is almost a hundred years old. Exact dates are not given.
The Ramnami Samaj is made a government-sanctioned organisation, according to Sahapedia.
Both traditions are declining. Sahapedia reports that the number of tattooed Ramnamis is falling fast, and Baiga girls now often decline the full tattoos.

future: Record Badnins and Ramnami elders on video, with their consent, naming each motif in their own words.
Pay the tattooists and teachers for workshops and for any use of their designs on cloth, prints and art.
Support young people who want to learn, without pressing them to be marked.
Keep a community-held archive of designs, so they are not taken as free decoration.
Teach schools and clinics about the meaning of godna, and challenge the idea that it is primitive.

name: Gond
tagline: Trees, animals and spirits drawn in dots and dashes.
facts: Medium: walls, canvas, paper
Tools: brush, pen and acrylic or poster colours
Signature: patterns of dots, lines and dashes (digna)
art: Gond art fills animals, birds, trees and deities with fine patterns of dots and lines that convey movement. Each form is alive because of its own pattern.
It draws on Gond belief that every hill, tree and animal has a spirit. Stories include the creation myths of the Gond people and local folk tales.
artist: Jangarh Singh Shyam (1962–2001), from Patangarh village, was discovered by the artist J. Swaminathan in the 1980s and went on to paint at Bharat Bhavan, Bhopal. He transformed Gond art from the ritual wall into the contemporary art world. He died in 2001 in Japan.
Many relatives and village artists from the Pardhan Gond community have followed him, including Bhajju Shyam and Durga Bai Vyam, whose work is widely published.
Our approach: honour Jangarh's legacy while profiling a new generation.
place: The Gond are among India's largest adivasi communities, living across central India. Patangarh is in the Dindori area of eastern Madhya Pradesh, near the Narmada, in sal forest country.
Forests are home, source of stories and now under pressure from mining and clearing.

history.what: Pardhans were bards and singers who recited Gond lore; ritual wall art decorated homes.
Jangarh Singh Shyam was brought to Bhopal; Bharat Bhavan gave him a platform.
His legacy has grown into a movement of Gond painters exhibiting worldwide.

future: Forest voices: let artists tell the forest's story for climate and conservation work.
Fair contracts for artists working with publishers and galleries.
A village museum in Patangarh to keep its own heritage.

name: Jadu Patua
tagline: The painter who brings back the eyes of the dead on a scroll.
facts: Form: scroll painting with song
Place: Naoasar village, Dumka
Scroll of 10 to 12 panels
Fewer than a dozen artists in the district
art: Jadu Patua, also spelled Jadu Patiya or Jadopatia, is a scroll painting of the Santhal Pargana. Each scroll has 10 to 12 paintings joined with homemade glue. The performer unrolls it, shows one painting at a time and sings the story, according to Village Square and The Better India.

The name is explained as jadu, meaning magician, and patia, meaning painter. Colours are natural: geru (red stone), sim leaves from broad beans and lamp black, mixed to make other shades. Brushes are made from thin twigs.

One use is ritual. Painters traditionally visited homes where someone had died. The picture of the dead person was drawn without pupils, and the family gave a gift (daan) so that the painter would paint the pupils in. Later scrolls showed the dead person happy in heaven, giving comfort to the family. Painters today also paint mythology and folklore.
artist: The Better India and Village Square report on three painters of Naoasar village in Masalia block, Dumka: Ganapati Chitrakar, Nitai Chitrakar and Jaydhan Chitrakar, whose late father Kamal Chitrakar was a noted artist. The ages given are from the time of the report.

Ganapati earned about Rs 150 to 200 a day, only in festival periods, and otherwise worked as a daily wager. The artists performed in Bhopal and Ahmedabad and were paid Rs 25,000 each, but the attention faded. Fewer than a dozen painters remain in the district, and few young people are learning.
place: Dumka is the headquarters of the Santhal Pargana in eastern Jharkhand, near the West Bengal border. The Naoasar painters live in a village of Hathiapathar panchayat, Masalia block.
The form is not confined to Jharkhand. Handicrafts sources place the tradition in West Bengal as well as the Santhal Pargana, and its patrons were Santhal and related communities.

history.what: Village Square calls it one of the oldest painting forms in the region. We found no dated record of its beginnings.
Painters visited Santhal and other homes with scrolls and songs, including after a death.

The Better India reports that the state Art and Culture Department kept no list of practising artists and that a minister said artists are called to perform in Ranchi on special occasions. An elder, Manik Chandra Mandal, asked for help to revive it.

future: Start a register of Jadu Patua artists, with their families and villages.
Fund the elder painters to teach, with a small regular stipend for students.
Document the funeral-scroll songs and the stories, with consent from the families who hold them.
Create steady paid performances and fair-priced sales beyond festivals.
Make natural colours and handmade glue easy to source, and support women and youth of the painter families to join.

name: Kalighat Painting
tagline: Bold brushstrokes from a temple street, from gods to gossip.
facts: Medium: paper, watercolour
Style: sweeping brush lines, flat bright colour
Subjects: deities, then social satire
art: Kalighat paintings, or pats, are bold and fast. Figures are outlined in one sweep of the brush, with a smooth shaded body. Early works showed Kali, Lakshmi and Krishna; later ones turned to everyday Calcutta life.
Satire became a strong theme, poking fun at the wealthy babu, at fashionable women and at scandals of the day.
artist: The painters were patuas, scroll-painters from rural Bengal who moved to Calcutta in the 19th century. They sold paintings to pilgrims at the Kali temple.
The style later inspired modern artists such as Jamini Roy.
Our approach: honour the patua community and its descendants, some of whom still paint in Bengal's villages.
place: Kalighat, in south Kolkata, is home to the Kali temple, one of the Shakti pithas. The temple grew from a riverside village into part of a colonial city.
The city's mix of pilgrims, clerks, merchants and colonial officials gave patuas their audience and their subjects.

history.what: Patuas settled near the Kalighat temple and began painting for pilgrims.
The style flourished and began to portray city life and satire.
Cheap lithographs and prints replaced hand-painted pats.
Museums hold collections, and Bengal's patuas continue their tradition.

future: Link museum collections to the patua families who inherit the tradition.
Commission new satire on today's city for a living tradition.
Keep street-level storytelling alive with temple-side workshops.

name: Kangra Miniature Painting
tagline: Soft lines, cool greens and the love of Radha and Krishna, painted in the hills below the Dhauladhar.
facts: Form: Pahari miniature painting, mineral and vegetable colours on paper
Peak: late 18th and early 19th century under Raja Sansar Chand
Main theme: Radha and Krishna, from the Gita Govinda and the Bhagavata Purana
GI registration: reported as 2012 (Wikipedia)
art: Kangra painting is a style of the Pahari, or hill, schools of miniature painting. It takes its name from the old Kangra state in what is now Himachal Pradesh. It grew out of the Guler school in the early 18th century and became famous in the later 18th century.

Its main subject is love, told through the story of Radha and Krishna. Painters drew on the Bhagavata Purana and Jayadeva's Gita Govinda. They also painted lovers (nayaka and nayika), the twelve months of the year (baramasa), and tales such as Nala and Damayanti.

The look is gentle. Lines are fine and faces are delicately modelled. Colours are cool and fresh, made from minerals and plants, and the surface has a glossy, enamel-like finish. Landscapes use many greens, flowering plants and streams, with a light pink for distant hills. Later works include night scenes and storms.
Pahari painting as a whole is dated from the early 17th to the mid 19th century. One survey calls Kangra the point where Pahari miniatures reach their finest and most creative work.
artist: Accounts say the style began in Guler, where painters trained in the Mughal manner, said to have come from Kashmir, found shelter at the court of Raja Dalip Singh (reigned 1695-1741). Their work was carried forward by Pandit Seu's sons, Nainsukh and Manaku, who are named among the great masters of the mid 18th century. Other names given are Khushala, Kishan Lal, Basia, Purkhoo and Fatoo.
Maharaja Sansar Chand Katoch (reigned 1776-1824) was the great patron. He commissioned many paintings on the life of Krishna, and the style reached its height at his court.

In modern times the state opened a training centre at Rait in 1973. Chandu Lal Raina, said to be a descendant of Pandit Seu and Nainsukh, led it until 1993 and trained 35 artists. The Kangra Arts Promotion Society in Dharamshala runs a school and workshop using traditional methods. In Chamba a long-running family lineage of painters, the Manikanth family, continues the tradition today, with Parkash Chand named as its present master.
place: Kangra lies in the Kangra valley at the foot of the Dhauladhar range. The old fort and the town of Kangra were the seat of the Katoch rulers. The Maharaja Sansar Chand Museum near Kangra Fort holds notable works.

The Pahari painting centres were Guler, Basohli, Chamba, Nurpur, Bilaspur and Kangra. The style later reached Mandi, Suket, Kullu, Arki, Nalagarh and Tehri Garhwal. Kangra paintings are also held in museums abroad, including the Rietberg in Zurich, the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the Metropolitan Museum and the Chester Beatty Library.

history.what: Painter families from Gujarat are said to have moved into the Punjab hills; the Manikanth family is recorded in Chamba around 1589.
The Rasamanjari illustrations, the earliest known Pahari-style series, date to about this time (Basohli).
The Guler style takes shape at the court of Raja Dalip Singh (1695-1741).
Nainsukh and Manaku, sons of Pandit Seu, are the leading masters of the age.
Sansar Chand rules Kangra and patronises Krishna paintings; the style peaks.
The Himachal government opens a training centre at Rait.
Kangra painting is reported to have received a Geographical Indication registration.
Writers describe the art as close to dying out because of cost, competition from digital art and thin support.

future: Training: more year-long courses like the Rait centre, with master-student pairing in Kangra and Chamba.
Livelihood: steady commissions, fair prices and GI-based labelling so that hand-painted work is not confused with prints.
Materials: keep mineral and plant pigments and handmade paper in use, and support the people who prepare them.
Documentation: digitise old works, as Project Srijan is doing, and record workshop methods from living painters.
Protection: use the GI registration, and care for the old collections in the Kangra and Chamba museums.

name: Kerala Mural Painting
tagline: Gods in five earth-and-leaf colours, painted on lime walls of temples and palaces.
facts: Medium: lime-plaster wall, painted with natural pigments
Palette: pancha varna, five colours (red, yellow, green, black, white)
Famous walls: Mattancherry, Padmanabhapuram, Ettumanoor, Krishnapuram
Training: Institute of Mural Painting, Guruvayur (1989)
art: Kerala's temple and palace murals are wall paintings of Hindu gods and stories: Vishnu, Krishna, Shiva, Devi and scenes from the Ramayana and Puranas. Most surviving examples are dated between about the 15th and 18th centuries, though some sites are older. Figures have large eyes, strong outlines, rich ornaments, and are framed by vines, flowers and cloth.

The traditional palette is called pancha varna, 'five colours': red, yellow, green, black and white. Writers describe red and yellow as coming from laterite earth, white from lime, black from lamp soot, and green from a plant-based mix that includes indigo-bearing leaves and a yellow tree resin or gamboge-type pigment. Binders such as tender coconut water and neem extract are named in several accounts. Scientific studies of old murals show that green in particular varied from one temple to another, so no single recipe fits every wall.

Colour also carries meaning. Several writers say the three gunas guide how a figure is coloured: gentle, godly (sattvic) figures are green, powerful and worldly (rajasic) ones red to golden-yellow, and fierce or dark (tamasic) ones black or white. This logic is described in modern books and surveys; we have not checked it against the old texts line by line, so treat it as the tradition's own account.

The technique is usually described as fresco-secco: pigment is applied on a lime plaster wall that is already prepared and mostly dry. One published account lists three plaster stages, the last with many fine washes of lime and tender coconut water. The work follows set stages: preparing the wall, drawing the outline, filling colour, and finishing with fine detail and ornament.

Painters are said to follow iconographic rules from texts such as the Chitrasutra (part of the Vishnudharmottara Purana), the Tantrasamuccaya (attributed to Narayana, 15th century) and Sri Kumara's Silparatna (16th century). These are named in standard surveys; how closely each wall follows them is a matter for specialists.
artist: The old painters of Kerala are mostly unnamed. Murals were made by trained guild-like workshops on the order of temples and rulers, and the art passed from teacher to student. Few signatures survive, so we do not name historical painters here.

The tradition weakened during the colonial period and, in several accounts, nearly died out. After Independence it was revived in a number of temples, and the Guruvayur Devaswom Board set up the Institute of Mural Painting at Guruvayur in 1989. Mammiyur Krishnan Kutty Nair is named as its first principal and as the leading figure of the modern revival; accounts differ on how credit for founding is shared with others at the Devaswom.

The institute offers a five-year National Diploma course in the gurukula spirit: two years of fine-art foundation, then three years of Kerala mural painting, with drawing, design, art history, and materials and methods. It admits about ten students a year, who are given scholarships and lodging. A Sanskrit university at Kalady also teaches the art.

Today trained painters work on temple walls, homes and public buildings, and also on canvas and panel. We would like to profile working painters by name with their consent; this draft does not yet name them.
place: Kerala is a narrow strip between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, with a hot, humid climate and two monsoons. Laterite earth, lime from shells, coconut and forest plants are all close at hand, which suits a craft made from them.

The murals are spread across the old kingdoms of Travancore, Kochi and Venad. Mattancherry Palace in Kochi, given to the Raja of Kochi by the Portuguese in the 16th century, has more than sixty Ramayana and other panels, according to Kerala Tourism. Padmanabhapuram Palace, built at the foot of the Veli hills, has 18th-century murals on its upper floor. It lies in Kanyakumari district of today's Tamil Nadu, but was Travancore's capital and is still owned and maintained by the Government of Kerala.

At Krishnapuram Palace near Kayamkulam, the Gajendra Moksham panel, Vishnu saving the elephant king, is described by Kerala Tourism as the largest mural panel in Kerala. Its size is quoted differently in different places, so we give no figure. Other key walls are at the Ettumanoor Shiva temple, the Vadakkunnathan temple in Thrissur (where Shiva panels are said to be over 350 years old), the Pundarikapuram temple, and the Thirunandikkara cave temple, now in Tamil Nadu, which is counted among the oldest surviving examples.
Guruvayur, one of Kerala's best-known Krishna temple towns, is where the training institute stands. The same damp air that makes the pigments from local plants also attacks the walls.

history.what: Cave and rock painting exists in Kerala, such as Edakkal and Marayoor, long before temple murals. The temple murals are a separate tradition.
The Thirunandikkara cave temple is counted among the oldest surviving mural sites; its exact date is debated.
The Tantrasamuccaya, a temple-building manual, is dated to this century in standard surveys.
The Silparatna of Sri Kumara is dated to this century. Mattancherry Palace was built or gifted by the Portuguese around the mid-1500s (sources give 1545 to 1557).
Murals spread across temples and palaces: Ettumanoor, Vadakkunnathan, Padmanabhapuram (rebuilt c. 1750) and Krishnapuram's Gajendra Moksham.
Royal patronage fades and the art declines under colonial rule.
Mattancherry Palace is declared a centrally protected monument; the ASI restores it again in 2007–2009.
The art is revived in several temples, led by painters such as Mammiyur Krishnan Kutty Nair.
The Guruvayur Devaswom Board founds the Institute of Mural Painting.
Scientific teams study old pigments to plan conservation, and trained painters keep the practice alive.

future: Site-by-site conservation: studies show different murals need different treatment, so each wall should have its own pigment and damage record.
Control damp and light in palaces and temples, and keep the walls open to worshippers and visitors without harming them.
A public digital archive with high-resolution photographs of every major wall, shared with temples and the Archaeology departments.
Support the Guruvayur institute and similar schools with apprenticeships, fair commissions and better pay for graduates.
Preserve the knowledge of making pigments and plaster, with documented recipes and small workshops.
Tell visitors the story at the site: guided walks that link Padmanabhapuram, Mattancherry, Krishnapuram and Guruvayur.

name: Kolam
tagline: A handful of rice flour at dawn, drawn around dots, gone by evening.
facts: Medium: rice flour (kolapodi), coloured powders
Built on a grid of dots called pulli
Main types: pulli kolam and sikku (knot) kolam
Redrawn daily; Margazhi is the big season
art: Kolam is a floor drawing made by pressing dry rice flour between thumb and finger and letting it fall in lines. Many designs start from a grid of dots, called pulli, which are joined or looped by lines. Sahapedia lists the six-pointed star, lotus, lamp, conch and pot among common symbols.

In sikku kolam, a continuous line loops around the dots and returns to where it began, like a knot. Both Sahapedia and Wikipedia describe the rule that every dot is circled and the lines close. Computer scientists and mathematicians have studied these rules, and Sahapedia mentions the scholar Gift Siromoney of Madras Christian College.

For special days, rice paste pressed through a cloth makes a longer-lasting kolam called makolam. Brick-red powder, kaavi, is often used for borders. Pongal, Deepavali, weddings, births and death rites each have their own kolams.

Sources give several reasons for the practice. Wikipedia says the flour feeds ants and birds, a form of welcoming guests. Sahapedia says it invites deities such as Lakshmi and Bhudevi and keeps misfortune away. Today stencils, rollers and stickers are also used.
artist: Kolam is mostly drawn by women, and the knowledge passes from mother to daughter. Sahapedia says women keep notebooks of difficult patterns to share. Sahapedia also notes that Jain and Paravar Catholic women draw kolam on special occasions.

Skill is judged by size and complexity. Wikipedia says that in the past women showed their skill by drawing large designs without lifting their hand, especially in Margazhi. Today some kolam artists also share their work on social media.
Our approach: record the women and the notebooks, with their own names for each pattern.
place: Kolam belongs to the thresholds of Tamil homes, temples and shops. It is drawn in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, and Wikipedia also notes similar practice in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and parts of Goa and Maharashtra, and among South Indian communities abroad.

Sahapedia says women draw it before dawn, and sometimes before dusk. The ground is swept, then sprinkled with water or a cow-dung and water mix. The threshold is seen as the meeting point of inside and outside.
The month of Margazhi (mid-December to mid-January) is the season most linked with kolam. Sahapedia and Wikipedia both say competitions are held then, for example at Mylapore in Chennai.

history.what: Sahapedia says the origins are unclear. Gift Siromoney argued that most threshold patterns are perhaps 600 years old, while some geometric designs may be far older.
A Tirunelveli inscription is the earliest textual reference Sahapedia names. It mentions temple women cleaning and decorating floors with kolam.
The Sanskrit text Stridharmapaddhati by Tryambakayajvan says household thresholds should bear ritual designs (Sahapedia).
The poems of Andal, the Tiruppavai, speak of women's ritual art. Sahapedia notes that she uses the term mandala.
Kolam competitions in Chennai and other cities, and online sharing, keep the art visible.

future: Teach children kolam in schools and community centres, along with its geometry.
Encourage natural rice flour and coloured powders from safe plant and mineral sources, in place of plastic stickers and chalk.
Pay women kolam artists fairly for festival and event work.
Collect and document pattern notebooks and oral names, with consent, in an open archive.
Support research that treats kolam as living heritage and credits the women who practise it.

name: Ladakhi Thangka
tagline: Rolled paintings of deities and mandalas, made in prayer and hung in the monasteries of the Indus valley.
facts: Form: painted or embroidered scroll on cotton, linen or silk
Pigments: minerals and plants, with gold for sacred details
Subjects: Buddhas, Tara, Avalokiteshvara, mandalas, the Wheel of Life
Giant thangkas are unfurled at festivals such as Hemis
art: A thangka is a Buddhist scroll painting. The Tibetan word is usually explained as 'something that can be rolled up'. It is kept rolled when not in use, and is mounted on silk brocade so it can be carried and stored. In Ladakh it is described as the central form of religious art.

The painter stretches cotton or silk on a frame and coats it with chalk and natural glue. The design is first drawn on a grid. Buddhist texts fix the proportions of each figure, so a Buddha or a Tara is drawn by rule, not by taste. Colours come from minerals, plants and semi-precious stones, and gold marks the most sacred parts. One painting can take weeks or months.

Common subjects are Buddha Shakyamuni, Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig), Tara, protector deities and mandalas. A mandala is a nested pattern of circles and squares around a central deity. The Bhavachakra, or Wheel of Life, shows the six realms of rebirth, held by Yama. Colours carry meaning: one source reads blue as wisdom, red as power and gold as enlightenment, and another reads white as purity and red as compassion. Different teachers explain the colours differently.

Thangkas are not decoration only. They are aids to meditation and teaching, and they are hung in monasteries and in household prayer rooms. Very large ones are unfurled on festival days. A source on Ladakh names Hemis, where large thangkas of Padmasambhava are shown during the festival.
artist: Thangka painters were traditionally monks, and in Ladakh young monks and apprentices still learn in monastery workshops under master painters. The training covers technique, Buddhist philosophy and iconography. Sources describe the making as a ritual act, with purification, prayer and mantra chanting, and a blessing by lamas when the painting is finished.

Today the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies (CIBS) and the Ladakh Arts and Media Organisation (LAMO) are named as places that train young artisans in traditional methods, natural pigments and iconometry, the system of sacred proportions.
We did not find named painters in the sources we read, so we leave them out.
place: Ladakh lies between India, Tibet and Central Asia, and its monasteries have long been places of learning as well as worship. Sources name Hemis, Thiksey, Spituk and Alchi among the places where thangka painting and sacred scrolls are found.
Hemis sits on the bank of the Indus about 45 km from Leh. Thiksey is known for its tall Maitreya figure and wall paintings. Alchi, further west, is also named as a place where the art flourished.

history.what: Popular accounts trace thangka roots to Indian Pala-period painting; others place the start of the form in Nepal around the 8th century. Scholars do not agree on a single origin.
The earliest surviving Tibetan cloth paintings that scholars cite date from around this time.
Ladakhi painters are described as blending Tibetan, Indian and Nepalese influences into their own style.
Monasteries, CIBS and LAMO run training. Cheap printed copies and synthetic materials are named as a threat to the craft.

future: Support apprenticeships so young painters can earn a living, since the long training puts many off.
Keep natural pigments in use and help pigment makers and cotton suppliers.
Photograph and document old thangkas in monastery stores, and teach safe storage in Ladakh's dry, cold climate.
Label printed copies as copies, so buyers can tell hand-painted work from prints.
Record the names of painters, so the makers are not forgotten.

name: Lepakshi Murals
tagline: Sixteenth-century ceilings in red ochre, lime white and lamp black, with a Veerabhadra over seven metres long.
facts: Period: 16th century, Vijayanagara style
Palette: red and yellow ochre, earth brown, lime white, lamp black, green
Patrons: Virupanna and Viranna
Temple is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India
art: The Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi has painted ceilings and walls from the Vijayanagara period. They show scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas, and forms of Shiva.

The IIACD documentation records the palette as red ochre, yellow ochre, earth brown, lime white, lamp black and green. Colours are laid flat and outlined in black or red ochre. Each scene is arranged around a centre, and figures are shown singly with little overlap, set apart by body colour, dress and ornament.

In the mukhamantapa is a large image of Veerabhadra, recorded at 7.7 by 4.3 m. IIACD calls it the largest single-figure painting of its period. Other writers use grander claims such as largest in Asia, and these claims conflict.

In the natyamantapa a cosmic lotus is at the centre of the ceiling. Around it are Kiratarjuniya in over fifteen scenes, the marriage of Parvati, and the story of Manuneeti Cholan, the longest single panel in the temple.
artist: The painters are not named in the sources I read. The murals are generally dated to the 16th century and probably belong to the same period as the temple.
Virupanna and Viranna, Vijayanagara officials, funded the temple. Panels show Virupanna and his brothers worshipping Veerabhadra, so the patrons are painted into the walls.
IIACD says the style is close to the ceiling paintings at the Chennakesava temple at Sompalem in Chittoor district.
place: Lepakshi is a village about 15 km east of Hindupur and about 120 km from Bengaluru. The temple stands on Kurmasila, a tortoise-shaped hill. It holds three shrines: Veerabhadra, Papanaseswara (Shiva) and Raghunatha (Vishnu).
A large monolithic Nandi bull stands at the village entrance, facing the temple. The Federal notes that the temple and the bull were added to India's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage in 2022.

history.what: IIACD notes an inscription dated 1493, in the reign of Saluva Immadi Narasimha, which mentions the Papanaseswara cave temple.

The Veerabhadra and Raghunatha shrines and the present Papanaseswara shrine seem to belong to the reign of Achyuta Deva Raya. Virupanna and Viranna funded them. Some writers give about 1538, and others 1530 or 1540, so the date is approximate.
The murals are dated to this century. Hanumantha Rao's book Lepakshi Temples (2004) is cited for this.
Some panels were retouched in later times, according to the Auro Society article.
The temple and Nandi were added to India's tentative UNESCO list, according to The Federal.

future: Restore the damaged panels with trained mural conservators. IIACD records bat damage in the Raghunatha shrine and The Federal reports that most panels outside the Veerabhadra figure are deteriorating.
Control bats, soot from lamps and damp, which are named as causes of damage.
Make a full digital record of every panel before more is lost.
Train local guides to explain the stories, and share the record with schools.
Protect the site through the ASI while involving the village, which depends on its visitors.

name: Madhubani
tagline: Walls of Mithila that became paper, and paper that travelled the world.
facts: Medium: walls, handmade paper, cloth
Pigments: natural dyes, rice paste, lampblack
Tools: bamboo nibs, twigs, fingers
art: Madhubani, also called Mithila painting, is known for dense, flat-colour figures with double-line borders and almost no empty space. Fish, birds, the sun and moon, lotuses, bamboo groves and scenes from the Ramayana and Krishna stories recur.

It was traditionally made by women on freshly plastered walls, especially the kohbar, the inner room where a newly married couple spends their first days. The images are blessings: fertility, abundance and union.
Scholars commonly describe several styles: Bharni (filled colour), Katchni (fine line work), Tantrik, Godna (tattoo-inspired) and Kohbar.
artist: Mithila painting was passed from mother to daughter and from aunt to niece. The painter was rarely credited by name because the work belonged to the household and the occasion.

That changed as the art moved to paper. Sita Devi, Ganga Devi and Mahasundari Devi became widely known and received Padma Shri honours, and Baua Devi was honoured in 2017. Today men also paint, and artists from different caste communities, once associated with distinct styles, now share and blend them.
Our approach: every artwork we feature should name its maker, her village and her story.
place: Mithila is a cultural region spanning northern Bihar and the adjoining Terai of Nepal. Madhubani is the district town most associated with the art; villages such as Jitwarpur and Ranti are known painting centres.

The land is a flood plain fed by the Kosi, Kamla and other Himalayan rivers. Fish, water and lotus imagery grows from that landscape, and the region's Maithili language, songs and Sita's legend as Mithila's daughter shape the stories told.

history.what: Oral tradition and literary references link Mithila with ritual floor and wall decoration. Sita's marriage in Mithila anchors much of the imagery.
After a major earthquake in Bihar, British colonial officer William G. Archer photographed paintings on the walls of damaged homes, bringing them to outside attention.
During a severe drought, the All India Handicrafts Board encouraged village women to paint on paper as an income source.
Artists such as Sita Devi and Ganga Devi gained national and international recognition and exhibited abroad.
Painting is a livelihood for many families, sold through cooperatives, fairs and online; the art has also spread to products and public murals.

future: Credit and pay: build direct-to-artist storytelling and fair pricing so the maker's name travels with the work.
Pass on the craft: partner with schools and village studios so younger painters learn both the traditional canon and new themes.
Safeguard authenticity: help buyers tell hand-painted work from prints.
Climate resilience: document flood-affected communities and support art-based income that does not depend on the farming season.
