name: Mandana Wall Art
tagline: White chalk designs on red clay, drawn by women to welcome blessings into the home.
facts: Medium: lime or chalk (khadiya) on red ochre (geru) and cow dung
Rajasthan: walls and floors; Madhya Pradesh: mostly floors
Makers: mainly Meena women
Tools: date-twig brush, hair or cotton
art: Mandana are wall and floor paintings from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. Wikipedia says they are drawn to protect hearth and home, to welcome the gods and to mark festivals and weddings.

The ground is clay plastered with cow dung and a local red clay or ochre. Designs are drawn in white lime or chalk, using cotton, a tuft of hair or a brush made from a date twig (Wikipedia; Utsavpedia).

Motifs include Ganesha, peacocks, women at work, tigers and flowers, along with geometric forms such as triangles and jaali lattices. Utsavpedia adds that newer designs show tractors, bullock carts and buses.
Utsavpedia says the art is traditionally done at Navratri and Diwali after the house is cleaned. It is linked to rangoli.
artist: Mandana is mainly made by Meena women, and skills pass from mothers to daughters by watching and copying (Utsavpedia). Wikipedia notes the Meena women of Hadoti in Rajasthan for their symmetrical, precise designs.
Wikipedia names Koshalya Devi of Baran as an artist who has helped conserve the traditional white-on-red style and who has painted over 100 designs on hardboard in oil.
Wikipedia and Utsavpedia both say the practice has become less visible. Utsavpedia says adapting the style to canvas has not revived it in villages.
place: In Rajasthan, mandana appears on both walls and floors. Utsavpedia names Tonk and Sawai Madhopur as places where it survives. In Madhya Pradesh it is mostly limited to floors, according to the same source.
In both states the art belongs to the home. Walls and courtyards are renewed with fresh clay at festival times, so each painting is temporary.

history.what: I found no reliable source for when mandana began; it is a household tradition passed on by women.
Drawn at Navratri, Diwali, weddings and births (Utsavpedia).
Madan Meena's book Nurturing Walls: Animal Paintings by Meena Women is published, as cited in Wikipedia.
The Hindustan Times reports on an artist struggling to keep the tradition alive, as cited by Wikipedia.
Designs are adapted to canvas, saris and salwar kameez fabrics (Utsavpedia).

future: Training: workshops where older women teach girls, in school or village.
Livelihood: pay women for commissioned work on cloth and canvas under their own names.
Materials: keep local ochre, chalk and clay in use.
Documentation: record designs and the names for them in each district, since Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh differ.
Protection: encourage villages to keep festival practice, which is what the art is for.

name: Manjusha Art
tagline: Snakes, a boat and a faithful wife, painted on temple-shaped boxes made for the snake goddess.
facts: Region: Anga, around Bhagalpur in eastern Bihar
Story: Bihula and the Bishahari sisters
Painted on boxes of bamboo, jute straw and paper, and on walls
Sources differ on age: 7th century is often cited, and some artists claim far older
art: Manjusha comes from a Sanskrit word for box. The boxes are temple-shaped and are used in Bishahari Puja, the worship of the snake goddesses in Bhagalpur. Sahapedia describes them as made of bamboo, jute straw and paper, and painted with scenes from the story of Bihula and the Bishahari sisters. The same story is painted on pots used in the worship and on house walls.

The story, as Sahapedia tells it, is this. Five Bishahari sisters sought worship from Chando Saudagar, a rich merchant of Champanagar and a devotee of Shiva. He refused. His six sons died at sea and the seventh, Bala Lakhendra, was bitten by a snake on his wedding night. His wife Bihula floated with his body on a boat, covered by a manjusha, to the world of the gods. She won back his life and the merchant agreed to worship the Bishaharis.

The look of the art is easy to spot. Human figures are drawn in an X shape with raised arms, large eyes and no ears. Borders carry motifs such as river ripples (leheriya), groups of snakes (sarp ladi), triangles and the bel leaf, which is sacred to Shiva. Sahapedia says each Bishahari sister is known by what she holds: a bow and arrow, a rising sun, a lotus, a mynah bird, or snakes in both hands. Outlines were traditionally drawn in green, though some artists now use black.
Writers call it a line drawing, a folk art and a scroll painting. It is often called Angika art or, by outsiders, snake painting.
artist: The art was made in the households around Bhagalpur. Sahapedia says the ceremonial boxes were traditionally made by Malakar families and the worship pots by Kumbhakar families. Women and men both painted murals in the worship space and in the rooms of newly married couples.

Several people are named as helping its revival. Chakravarty Devi, from a Malakar family, organised artisans and received the Bihar Kala Award (the Sita Devi Award). Basant Pandit and Chhedi Pandit, Kumbhakar artists of Champanagar, are credited with reviving the work. Manoj Pandit, a fine arts graduate, tried new materials and was given the title Manjusha Kala Guru by the Ministry of Culture in 2014. Other artists named include Nirmala Devi, Ulupi Jha and Soma Roy.
Today artists also paint on silk and other fabrics and make more abstract pieces, while keeping the religious motifs.
place: Manjusha belongs to Anga, the old region of eastern Bihar whose capital Champa lies near today's Bhagalpur. Sahapedia notes that rivers separated Anga from neighbouring Magadha and Vajji, which is one reason given for the art staying so local.

Bhagalpur is on the Ganga. The Bishahari Puja is held there and in nearby areas. The Bihula-Bishahari story is also sung as an oral gatha, though Sahapedia says it is now less popular. Manjusha work is seen on some government buildings in Bhagalpur, and workshops have been held under the Bhagalpur Smart City project.

history.what: Anga is named in early texts. Sahapedia says Champa was its capital and that Magadha under Bimbisara annexed it in the 6th century BC.

Wikipedia, citing a promotional foundation, says the art dates to the 7th century. Some artists, quoted by Sahapedia, link it to the Indus period (about 2600 BC) because of snake terracottas found at Karnagarh. This second claim is the artists' own and is not firmly established.
Sahapedia says W.G. Archer, an ICS officer, documented the paintings and his collection was shown at the India Office Library in London.
Sahapedia says patronage fell and the art nearly died out.
The Bihar government's public relations department revived interest through slide shows in villages.
Disha Gramin Vikas Manch worked with NABARD to build livelihoods through the art.
Awards were given to Manjusha artists, including the Manjusha Kala Guru title in 2014.

future: Training: workshops for young painters, so the Malakar and Kumbhakar knowledge is not lost
Livelihood: new products on fabric and paper, with fair prices to the artist
Materials: keep the boxes, bamboo and natural colours alive for worship, not only for sale
Documentation: record the Bihula-Bishahari gatha, which is now sung less
Protection: seek recognition such as a GI tag, if the community wants it, to separate genuine Bhagalpur work from copies

name: Medinipur Patachitra
tagline: Painted scrolls that are sung as they unroll, from the patuas of Naya.
facts: Scroll painting on cloth, sung while shown (pater gaan)
Painters are called patuas, often with surname Chitrakar
Bengal Patachitra received a GI tag in 2018
About 300 patuas live in Naya, according to Down To Earth
art: A patachitra is a painted scroll. The patua unrolls it a section at a time and sings a song that tells what each picture shows. Wikipedia quotes that every patachitra has a song to go with it.

Subjects include the Ramayana and Mahabharata, Radha-Krishna, Chaitanya, Kali and Shiva, and Bengali tales such as Manasa, Chandi and Behula-Lakhindar. Some scrolls tell news and social issues, such as dowry. Naya's recent scrolls have shown COVID-19 and strong women.

Colours come from plants and minerals. Wikipedia lists chalk for white, pauri for yellow, indigo for blue, bhushakali for black and sindur for red. Down To Earth adds that artists now also use modern paint and varnish to make scrolls last. Wikipedia says Medinipur scrolls are known for large seated figures.
artist: Patuas have been scroll painters and singers for generations. Down To Earth describes Naya, where Swarna Chitrakar is a role model; she overcame poverty and discrimination and keeps the art alive, with her husband and daughter. In 2018 she showed her work at a UNESCO General Assembly in Paris.

Wikipedia notes Manimala Chitrakar for bold colour and a personal iconography. Folklibrary says the project covering patachitra included about 380 artists from Paschim Medinipur and 319 from Purba Medinipur.
Artists sell online and take custom orders, and Pingla has become a known market.
place: Naya is in Pingla block, Paschim Medinipur. Down To Earth says the nearest railway station is 11 km away. The village is far from big towns, yet scrolls from Naya are held in the National Museum of Ethnology in Lisbon, according to Wikipedia.
Medinipur lies in the lower Ganga plain of south-west Bengal. Purulia, Birbhum and Bankura also have patachitra traditions with their own colour schemes.

history.what: Wikipedia says the dating is disputed, with some sources linking it to the pre-Pala period from the historical themes in songs.
Patachitra is included in a Ministry of Textiles craft cluster project, per Folklibrary.
Bengal Patachitra receives a GI tag. The tag covers Bengal as a whole, not only Medinipur.

future: Training: teach young patuas the song as well as the painting.
Livelihood: keep direct online and custom sales, led by women artists.
Materials: record and keep plant and mineral colour recipes beside modern paints.
Documentation: record scroll songs and their painters.
Protection: use the GI to separate hand-painted scrolls from printed copies.

name: Mewar and Kishangarh Miniature Painting
tagline: Bold, flat colour in Mewar; long-eyed, devotional elegance in Kishangarh.
facts: Two Rajput court schools of Rajasthan
Mewar: earliest dated work is the Chawand Ragamala of 1605
Kishangarh: best known for Nihal Chand's Bani Thani
Both patronised by royal courts
art: Mewar and Kishangarh are two of the Rajasthani courts that produced miniature paintings under Rajput rulers. Their styles are very different.

Wikipedia's account of Mewar painting calls it a conservative idiom: bright colour, flat forms, abstract shapes and bold line. Early works were manuscripts. Later, at Udaipur, court paintings grew larger and recorded durbars, festivals, hunts and temple visits.

Kishangarh painting is known for slender figures with long necks, arched eyebrows, lotus-shaped eyes and a pointed nose and chin. The themes are Krishna's life and the epics, in the moods of bhakti (devotion) and shringara (romance). Colours include white, yellow and pink, and the materials include handmade paper (basli), a chalk ground (khadiya) and natural pigments.
The best-known Kishangarh picture is the portrait called Bani Thani, often called the Indian Mona Lisa. That nickname is popular, not scholarly.
artist: Mewar names are well documented. Nasiruddin painted the Chawand Ragamala in 1605. Sahibdin (active 1628-55) led the workshop under Jagat Singh I and worked on a large Ramayana with Manohar. Later names include the Stipple Master (active c. 1692-1715, anonymous), Jai Ram, Bagta, Chokha, Baijnath and Tara.

Kishangarh's leading painter was Nihal Chand (1710-1782), credited with the Bani Thani portraits and with beginning to show the royal couple as Krishna and Radha. Some sources say Sawant Singh sketched the ideas himself; this is not settled.
In the 19th century, Nathdwara painting centred on the Shrinathji temple. Ghasiram Sharma (1869-1932) carried its devotional style into the 20th century.
place: Mewar was based first around Chittor and later Udaipur in southern Rajasthan. It was the last Rajput state to accept Mughal overlordship, in 1615, according to Wikipedia. Painting also flourished at Deogarh and at Nathdwara.

Kishangarh is a small princely town in central Rajasthan, near Ajmer. Its courts used the town's lakes and palaces as the settings of its paintings, with turquoise lakes, terraced gardens and marble pavilions, as EBSCO describes.

history.what: The Chawand Ragamala by Nasiruddin is the earliest dated Mewar work.
Mewar accepts Mughal suzerainty after long resistance.
Under Jagat Singh I, Sahibdin leads a large output including a Bhagavata Purana (1648) and a Ramayana (1649-53).
Udaipur court painting develops: the Stipple Master under Amar Singh II, large durbar scenes under Sangram Singh II and Jagat Singh II.
Sawant Singh begins to rule Kishangarh. EBSCO gives his death as 1764 and 30 Stades gives his reign as 1748-57, so sources differ on when it ended.
Nihal Chand paints Bani Thani and the couple as Radha and Krishna. EBSCO notes some finest works were made in the decade or so after Sawant Singh's death.
The Kishangarh school largely ends.
Royal patronage in Mewar ends with the end of princely powers.

future: Support schools and workshops that teach traditional miniature technique: paper preparation, natural pigments and fine brush work.
Pay painters fairly for original work, and make copies and prints clear as copies.
Digitise manuscripts and paintings held in palaces, museums and private collections, with open access and local-language notes.
Name the painters in exhibitions and labels, not only the rulers.
Protect natural pigments and handmade paper makers who supply the studios.

name: Mughal Miniature Painting
tagline: Court painting made in imperial workshops, from Persian roots to portraits, animals and emperors.
facts: Period: roughly 1530s to the 18th century
Roots: Persian miniature painting
Medium: opaque watercolour and gold on paper
Hamzanama: about 1,400 cotton folios, worked on 1562 to 1577
art: Mughal painting grew from Persian miniature painting and became almost entirely secular, with a strong interest in portraits, animals and plants. It was made for the court, to illustrate books and to record the emperor's life.

Works were done in opaque watercolour and gold on paper, then mounted in borders and placed between decorated covers. Wikipedia describes a team method. Senior artists outlined the composition, junior artists applied colour, and specialists sometimes painted faces.

The Hamzanama is the great early project. According to Wikipedia it was worked on from 1562 to 1577, on about 1,400 cotton folios, each about 69 by 54 cm. It helped merge artists from Iran and different parts of India into one style.

Under Jahangir the brushwork became finer and the colours lighter, with European influence on perspective and a taste for nature studies. Under Shah Jahan, court painting became more formal, with the emperor shown in strict profile. The Padshahnama, now at Windsor, was painted on gold-flecked paper.
artist: Wikipedia names several painters. Basawan was active around 1580 to 1600, and his son Manohar Das around 1582 to 1624. Daswanth, who died in 1584, worked on the Razmnama. Ustad Mansur, active around 1590 to 1624, was a specialist in animals and plants. Bichitr, active around 1610 to 1660, was a portraitist with European influence.

Akbar liked artists' names to be written below the paintings. This is why scholars can attribute many works to named hands. He hired over one hundred painters between 1570 and 1585, according to the same page.
Humayun brought the Persian artists Abd al-Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali to India after his exile at the Safavid court. Akbar studied painting under Abd al-Samad.
place: The imperial workshops moved with the court. Wikipedia places the early work in Delhi and Agra, and Akbar's reign includes Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra in Uttar Pradesh. I did not find a source on the exact location of each workshop, so the map pins mark these cities in general.
After the Mughal court weakened, many painters moved to Rajput courts. This is how Mughal ideas flowed into Rajasthani painting, and why Rajasthan is in this entry's state line.
Large collections of Mughal paintings are held in museums in India and abroad. The Padshahnama is in the Royal Collection at Windsor.

history.what: Humayun is exposed to Persian miniatures in exile and brings Abd al-Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali to India.
The Tutinama shows the imperial style taking shape.
The Hamzanama is made under Akbar.
Akbar hires more than a hundred painters, per Wikipedia.
Under Jahangir, finer brushwork, portraits and natural-history studies.
Under Shah Jahan, a formal style. The Padshahnama is painted.
Aurangzeb probably commissioned no paintings after about this date.
A short revival under Muhammad Shah. By the time of Shah Alam II (1759 to 1806) its earlier standing is gone, and Rajput and Company painting take over.

future: Training: a few families and art schools still teach miniature techniques, but I did not find a specific source on Mughal-style training today.
Livelihood: modern miniature painters sell copies and new work in Delhi, Agra and Jaipur. The market mixes careful work with cheap copies.
Materials: mineral and plant pigments, gold, and handmade paper are costly. Supporting small suppliers keeps the methods alive.
Documentation: digitising museum folios, with the names of artists where known, helps study and teaching.
Protection: original folios need controlled light and humidity. Illegal trade in manuscript leaves is a concern for museums.

pins.label: Jaipur, Rajasthan (Rajput courts took in Mughal-trained painters)

name: Mysore Painting
tagline: Serene gods in gold leaf, from the court of the Wodeyars.
facts: Medium: paper pasted on wood or cloth
Materials: gesso, gold leaf, natural pigments
Subject: Hindu gods, goddesses and court scenes
art: Mysore paintings are known for their gentle, calm figures with delicate faces, soft shading and fine gold leaf. Gods and goddesses sit in decorated arches amid floral borders.
A raised gesso paste is applied to ornaments before gilding, which gives the jewellery a relief look, and every layer is done by hand.
artist: The art is made by trained painters, many from families in Mysuru, who follow strict rules for the proportions and colours of each deity.
A single painting can take weeks or months.
Our approach: show the process, layer by layer.
place: Mysuru was the seat of the Wodeyar rulers, known for palaces, silk, sandalwood and the Dasara festival.
The city remains a major cultural centre in southern Karnataka.

history.what: The style has roots in painting traditions of the Vijayanagara empire.
The Mysore court supported painters and the style flowered.
A small number of studios keep the tradition.

future: Offer apprenticeships to younger painters.
Rely on sustainable gold-leaf sourcing.
Let visitors see the stages in open workshops.

name: Nirmal Paintings and Toys
tagline: Gold-touched paintings and soft-wood toys from the Naqash families of Nirmal.
facts: Makers: Naqash (Nakkash) artisans
Toys: soft poniki wood, painted and oiled
Paintings: lacquered wood, bright colours, a touch of gold
GI: toys tagged in 2008 per one source; others say 2009
art: Nirmal is known for two related crafts. Nirmal paintings are made on lacquered wooden boards, often with a black ground, in bright colours with gold touches. Nirmal toys are small painted wooden figures of fruit, birds, animals and village people.

For the paintings, the artist coats the wood, traces a design in chalk, fills it with colour, adds gold and varnishes it. Wikipedia says colours came from minerals, herbs and plants. Outlook Traveller adds that the style shows Ajanta, Mughal and Rajasthani miniature influence, and that a touch of gold marks Nirmal work.

For the toys, the main wood is poniki (Givotia rottleriformis), a soft white wood from Adilabad forests. Pieces are sun-dried and joined with lappam, a paste of sawdust and tamarind seed powder. A coat of glue and river silt gives a white base. Painting is now mostly with enamel, and the finish is groundnut oil, according to an excerpt from a book on Nirmal toys published by ThePrint.
Themes are mythology, folk tales, flowers and everyday life. Craftspeople now also paint furniture and utility goods.
artist: The makers are the Naqash community. The toy makers are described as the Somakshatriya subgroup. Accounts of how they came to Nirmal differ. One names a 17th-century general, Nimmal Naidu, who founded a weapons foundry. The community itself says it arrived during Vijayanagara rule. Another feature says a chieftain brought them from Rajasthan, but that their origins are lost in antiquity.

Nirmal was a weapons centre until Hyderabad's annexation in 1948 ended the Nizam's patronage. Since 1955 a state-funded cooperative has supported the artisans, and most now work through it. Some women work from home.
Our approach: name the cooperative's painters and toy makers and show who paints which part.
place: Nirmal is a town in Nirmal district, northern Telangana, about 220 km by road from Hyderabad. Basara, about 70 km away, has more places to stay.
The poniki wood comes from forests in Adilabad district. ThePrint's excerpt says present rules let artisans collect only fallen trees, which makes the wood harder and costlier to find.

history.what: The government handicrafts portal and Wikipedia say Naqash artisans practised the art as early as the 14th century.
Some writers link the art to the Kakatiya period. Sources differ and this is not firmly documented.
A general named Nimmal Naidu is said to have founded a weapons foundry at Nirmal.
Hyderabad's annexation ends the Nizam's patronage.
Wikipedia says Lady Hyderi brought the artisans to Hyderabad state and promoted the craft.
A state-funded cooperative begins to support the artisans.
Nirmal toys receive a GI tag; sources differ on the year.

future: Training: courses for new learners, already run by the state and NGOs, with paid apprenticeships.
Livelihood: new products and fair prices so that painting pays as well as other work.
Materials: planted poniki stock and safe pigments, as wood and natural colours are hard to get.
Documentation: record traditional designs and colour recipes.
Protection: guard the GI and label genuine pieces. Reports say toy-making families fell from about 200 to 40.

name: Pahari Wall Painting
tagline: Murals in hill temples and bridal rooms, where the miniature painter's world meets the wall.
facts: Form: murals on temple and house walls in the Pahari region
Example: Devi Kothi temple, Chamba, built in the reign of Raja Umed Singh (1748-64)
Related: bangadwari, wedding-room wall paintings of Chamba
Style link: Chamba miniature painting
art: Pahari wall painting is the mural side of the hill painting tradition. It is found in temples, forts and houses of the Himalayan foothills, painted by artists who also worked in miniature.

At the Devi Kothi temple in Chamba, murals show Devi and Krishna slaying demons. They are influenced by Chamba miniature painting, with only primary colours. Sahapedia says the Krishna scenes on the eastern wall follow episodes from Laharu's Bhagavata paintings. The carved wooden ceiling shows mythological and celestial beings.

Chamba's nuptial wall paintings, called bangadwari, retain features of 16th-century northern Indian art. Under the Dogras, temples and forts were decorated with murals, such as those at Krimchi, Babbor and Bahu fort.

A Sahapedia article on murals at Sui and Burj temples in Jammu says Pahari murals were painted on lime plaster with pigments from marble, soot and indigo. I have not confirmed that the same method was used everywhere in Himachal.
artist: The temple murals I read do not name their painters. Sahapedia describes the Devi Kothi murals as influenced by the Chamba miniature tradition, so the painters were probably from the same circles, but this is an inference.
Chamba's painter families, such as the Manikanth family settled around 1589, worked in miniatures. Whether they painted particular walls I could not confirm.
Because wall paintings are rarely signed, this entry names no individual wall painters.
place: Chamba, on the Ravi, has many temples and a museum, the Bhuri Singh Museum, with Pahari paintings. Devi Kothi lies on the northern edge of the old Chamba kingdom.
Wall paintings in bridal rooms are also reported in Kangra, Mandi and Bilaspur. One non-scholarly source says some survived the 1905 earthquake; I treat that as unconfirmed.

history.what: One scholar dates the origins of Pahari painting in Chamba to this period (Wikipedia, citing Ohri).
Pahari painting flourishes in the hills.
Devi Kothi temple is built under Raja Umed Singh of Chamba.
Temples and forts in the region are decorated with murals.

future: Training: train local conservators and painters in lime plaster and mineral pigment methods.
Livelihood: temple-visit trails that bring income to villages that hold murals.
Materials: use compatible lime and natural pigments when repairing.
Documentation: survey and photograph murals village by village, since many remain unrecorded.
Protection: involve temple committees and the Archaeological Survey and state departments in care.

name: Paitkar Scroll Painting
tagline: Painted scrolls unrolled one panel at a time while the painter sings.
facts: Form: scroll painting with song
Village: Amadubi, East Singhbhum
Colours from stones, leaves and soot
Few families still practise it
art: Paitkar paintings are scrolls made of several panels. The painter unrolls one panel at a time and sings the story it shows. The Handicrafts Ministry page, the Rural India Online report and Village Square all describe the painting and the song as a pair.

Stories include the origin of the Santhals and of life, village scenes and festivals, the dances Karma and Baha, the epics, and deities such as Durga, Kali and Manasa. Paintings once reached 12 to 14 feet. Today they are mostly about A4 size.

Rural India Online describes the colours: red from stone rubbed on a wet slab, yellow from turmeric, green from beans or chillies, violet from lantana fruit and black from lamp soot. Paper has largely replaced cloth. Neem or babool resin is added to protect the work from insects.
artist: The painters belong to Chitrakar families, and the singers to Gayen families, according to Village Square, which counts about 45 artisans in Amadubi. Outlook Traveller puts it at around 54 painter families. The figures differ, so treat them as approximate.

Rural India Online names Anil Chitrakar, aged 71 in the report, as the village's oldest painter, who learned music from his father. Vijay Chitrakar learned from his grandfather. Anjana Patekar is one of the few women painters.

Traditionally artists travelled to villages during festivals, selling paintings and singing, as far as Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. Rural India Online reports that mobile phones and recorded music have reduced demand for live singing, and that young people have left for wage work.
place: Amadubi (spelled Amadobi in some sources) is a village near Dhalbhumgarh and Ghatshila in East Singhbhum district, in south-east Jharkhand. Distances given to Jamshedpur differ across sources, from about 65 to 70 km.

In 2013 the state government and the non-profit Kalamandir set up the Amadubi Rural Tourism Centre. Artists told Village Square it has brought few buyers. Kalamandir's founder disagrees that the art is fading and says it is seeking a GI tag.

history.what: Rural India Online says the art came from West Bengal and Jharkhand and was influenced by pandulipi manuscript scrolls. No written record exists, so its age is not known.

Village Square reports that artisans trace their settlement to King Ramchandra Dhal of Dhalbhumgarh, who gave land to travelling painters and singers. This is the artisans' account and we found no other confirmation.
The Amadubi Rural Tourism Centre was set up by the state government and Kalamandir.
Rural India Online reports that over 40 households once painted in the village and only a few do now. Village Square says the pandemic stopped paid workshops and pushed artists into other work.

future: Pay artists to train young people in both painting and singing, since the two go together.
Keep scrolls long and in cloth or paper made for the purpose, not only small souvenir sheets.
Record the songs with the senior singers and their families, with the story texts written down.
Build steady buyers and fair prices for the artists, with the work marketed beyond the tourism centre.
Help artists get natural colour materials, and bring the village onto an arts trail in the festival season.
Support women painters in the family to work openly and sell their work.

name: Pattachitra
tagline: Cloth scrolls of Lord Jagannath, painted with stone, shell and soot.
facts: Medium: cloth coated with tamarind-seed gum and chalk
Pigments: minerals, shell, lampblack, plant colours
Tools: brushes from animal hair
art: Pattachitra (from patta, cloth, and chitra, picture) is a detailed narrative painting. Bold outlines, rich borders and expressive eyes frame stories of Jagannath, Krishna and Rama and the Puri temple's rituals.

Craftsmen prepare their own canvas by pasting layers of cloth with tamarind seed paste and chalk, then polishing it smooth. Colours are made from natural sources such as white from burnt conch shell, black from lamp soot and red from ochre.
artist: The painters are called chitrakars. Skills pass within families and are linked to the Jagannath temple, where painters create the deity's sacred images and ornaments.
Raghurajpur, near Puri, is a heritage craft village where nearly every home is also a studio, and children learn alongside their parents.
Our approach: profile a household at a time, including the women who prepare canvases and colours.
place: Puri on the Bay of Bengal is one of the four dhams and home to the Rath Yatra. Raghurajpur lies in a palm-fringed grove on the Bhargavi river banks nearby.
Cyclones regularly hit the Odisha coast, so houses, studios and materials are repeatedly at risk.

history.what: Painted images tied to the cult of Jagannath developed in Odisha; paintings were made as souvenirs for pilgrims.
Revived with government support and craft fairs; Raghurajpur was developed as a heritage craft village.
Artists also paint on palm leaf, tussar silk and products, while temple-linked commissions continue.

future: Storm-proof the archive: digitise heirloom scrolls and recipes for natural colours.
Cyclone recovery fund: help the village rebuild studios quickly after storms.
Pilgrim-to-patron path: turn the pilgrim souvenir market into long-term relationships with artists.

name: Phad
tagline: A temple on a scroll, carried by singers from village to village.
facts: Medium: long cloth scrolls (phad)
Subject: epics of Pabuji and Devnarayan
Performers: Bhopas and Bhopis
art: A phad is a long painted cloth, sometimes many metres wide, crowded with a single epic. The folk deities Pabuji and Devnarayan are the heroes, and the entire narrative is spread across the cloth in colour-coded scenes.
The scroll is a portable shrine. At night, a bhopa singer and his wife sing the epic by lamplight and point to each scene as the story unfolds.
artist: The painters are the Joshi family of the Chhipa community. The art centres around Shahpura and Bhilwara.
Shree Lal Joshi received a Padma Shri in 2006 and set up the Joshi Kala Kunj / Chitrashala in Bhilwara to train people outside the family, opening a closed tradition.
Our approach: record the full performance, painter and singer together.
place: The Marwar and Mewar regions of Rajasthan are dry, with a strong tradition of itinerant bards and folk heroes.
Pabuji is revered as a protector of camels and cattle, a hero for herding communities.

history.what: Phad painting grew alongside the performance tradition.
The Joshis opened the craft to new students and began making smaller paintings for sale.
Fewer villages commission full performances, so the art is shifting to galleries and homes.

future: Keep the performance alive: fund bhopa-bhopi performances, not only paintings.
Record the epics, in the singers' own voices, as an open archive.
Pair each painting with a QR audio of the song.

name: Pichwai
tagline: The cloth that dresses a god's wall, painted for each season.
facts: Medium: cloth, hand-painted
Subject: Shrinathji, Krishna with cows and lotus
Context: Pushtimarg tradition
art: Pichwai means 'that which hangs at the back'. These large cloths hang behind the image of Shrinathji, a form of Krishna lifting Mount Govardhan.
Different festivals have different designs: lotus ponds for summer, cows and cowherds for Gopashtami, and the grand Annakut mountain of food.
artist: Pichwai painters work in Nathdwara's family workshops, many trained from childhood. A single large pichwai can involve several artists, each handling a task such as outline, gold work or faces.
Our approach: acknowledge the full team on every piece.
place: Nathdwara in the Aravalli hills near Udaipur became a pilgrimage centre when the Shrinathji image was moved here from the Braj region in the 17th century to protect it. It has remained the heart of the Pushtimarg sect.
The entire town's economy is tied to the temple.

history.what: The Shrinathji image was moved to Mewar under the Maharana's protection; the temple town grew.
Nathdwara's painters developed into a flourishing school under temple patronage.
Pichwai has reached global fashion and design, sometimes without community credit.

future: Protect both the sacred use and the market work, with clear guidelines.
Credit workshops by name on every product line.
Digitise the festival calendar so the cycle of designs is not forgotten.

name: Pithora
tagline: A wall of horses painted to give thanks to the god.
facts: Medium: house walls, now paper and canvas
Ground: prepared cow-dung and clay wall
Subject: Baba Pithora and a procession of horses
art: Pithora is a ritual wall painting of the Rathwa, Bhil and Bhilala communities. The walls of a home's main room fill with horses, deities, riders, sun, moon, trees and animals in bright colours.
It is painted to give thanks after a wish has been granted, such as a good harvest, a birth or recovery from illness. Horses are the key symbol.
artist: The painting is led by a priest-painter, the lakhara, who learns the mythic chant and the images. The family and neighbours help.
As the painting is a vow and a ceremony, it is made once and left for the elements.
Our approach: record the ritual with permission from the community.
place: Chhota Udepur in eastern Gujarat and Jhabua in western Madhya Pradesh sit in a hilly tribal belt along the border.
Farming, forests and festivals structure community life.

history.what: Pithora has long been painted in village homes by Rathwa and Bhil communities.
Collectors and cultural bodies noticed the art and artists began to paint on paper.
Both ritual and gallery versions exist.

future: Protect the ritual from commercial copying.
Fund documentation of the chants as well as the images.
Support the next generation of lakharas.

name: Rajput Miniature Schools
tagline: Court schools of Mewar, Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh, Jaipur and more, each with its own hand.
facts: Period: late 16th to mid-19th century
Name: introduced by Ananda Coomaraswamy in 1916
Medium: gouache on paper
Themes: Ragamala, Krishna stories, Ramayana, heroine types
art: Rajput painting is the court painting of the Hindu Rajput states. It is divided into Rajasthani and Pahari (hill) styles. The name was introduced by Ananda Coomaraswamy in 1916. This entry covers the Rajasthani and Malwa schools.

The medium is gouache, opaque watercolour on paper. Wikipedia describes the stages as a charcoal sketch, black outline, layered colour, burnishing, and last details such as gold. Common themes are Ragamalas (pictures of musical modes), episodes of Krishna from the Bhagavata Purana, the Ramayana, and types of heroine from Hindi poetry.

Each court had its own look. Mewar is the most traditional. Bundi's fine line and calm palette owe much to Mughal painting. Kota is known for large hunting scenes. Bikaner blends Mughal polish with a Deccani-influenced palette. Marwar has early landmarks such as the Pali Ragamala of 1623. Malwa, once called Primitive Rajasthani, uses flat colour blocks and vermilion. Sirohi has strong colours and bold contour lines.

Kishangarh is famous for slender faces with large upturned eyes. Jaipur's school peaked under Pratap Singh (r. 1778 to 1803), with a 43-painting Ragamala and a Bhagavata Purana of 1792 with 366 illustrations.
artist: Many painters are known by name. At Mewar, Nisardin painted the Chawand Ragamala in 1605, and Sahibdin worked under Jagat Singh I on the large Ramayana of 1649 to 1653. At Bikaner, Ruknuddin was the best known painter. At Kishangarh, Bhavanidas came from Delhi in 1719 and taught Nihal Chand (c. 1710 to 1782), whose work is seen as the classic Kishangarh idiom. At Jaipur, Sahibram was a leading portraitist.

Wikipedia says Savant Singh of Kishangarh (r. 1748 to 1764), a poet and Krishna devotee, is linked to the classic style, and that his companion Bani Thani is supposedly the model for Radha. The word supposedly matters here, as this is tradition and not firm record.

Patrons were the royal courts. When courts lost power, painters lost their work. Royal patronage in Mewar ended with the abolition of princely powers in 1949. Nathdwara painting continued through temple patronage.
place: The schools belong to the old kingdoms of Rajasthan and the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh: Mewar (Udaipur), Bundi, Kota, Bikaner, Marwar (Jodhpur), Sirohi, Kishangarh and Jaipur (Amber). Each court had its workshop and its own taste.

Mewar accepted Mughal rule only in 1615. Bikaner submitted to Akbar in 1570. This helps explain why some schools look closer to Mughal work than others. In 1728 Sawai Jai Singh moved his capital to Jaipur and built a complex for the arts of the book.
Nathdwara, near Udaipur, is linked to the temple painting that outlasted the courts. Pins for Malwa are approximate because the sources I read name the style, not one exact town.

history.what: Bikaner submits to Akbar (1570) and Mewar accepts Mughal rule (1615). Contact with Mughal painting grows.
Early Ragamalas: the Chunar Ragamala (1591) and the Chawand Ragamala (1605).
The Pali Ragamala of Marwar, by Pandit Virji.
The large Mewar Ramayana, in which Sahibdin and Manohar worked.
The Narsyang Shahar Ragamala by Madho Das marks the peak of the Malwa style.
Kishangarh under Raj Singh (r. 1706 to 1748). Bhavanidas arrives in 1719.
Sawai Jai Singh moves his capital to Jaipur.
Photography and imported pigments reduce court patronage. Kota and Bundi schools fade by the end of the century, per Wikipedia.

future: Training: miniature painting is taught in Udaipur, Jaipur, Bundi and Kishangarh workshops, though I found no specific source on numbers.
Livelihood: painters sell to tourists and collectors. Fine hand work competes with printed copies.
Materials: mineral colours, gold leaf and burnished handmade paper take skill and cost. Reliable supply helps keep them in use.
Documentation: museums and royal collections hold many works with artists' names. Joint catalogues across collections would help.
Protection: older folios are fragile. Careful storage and digital copies reduce handling.

name: Rangoli
tagline: Floor designs at the doorstep, drawn fresh each day and left for feet, wind and ants.
facts: Form: floor drawing in powder, flour, petals or paint
Names: kolam, muggu, alpana, mandana, aipan, pookkalam and more
Makers: traditionally women, passed from mother to daughter
Origin of the word: Sanskrit ranga, colour
art: Rangoli is the art of drawing patterns on the ground, most often at the entrance of a home. The word comes from the Sanskrit ranga, meaning colour. Almost every region has its own name and style for it. It is called kolam in Tamil Nadu, muggu in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, alpana in West Bengal, mandana in Rajasthan, aipan in Uttarakhand, saathiyo in Gujarat and pookkalam in Kerala.

Materials are simple. Wikipedia lists powdered limestone, red ochre, dry rice flour, coloured sand, flower petals and brick powder. Turmeric and vermilion give colour. Today crayons, acrylic paint and coloured cement are also used.

Styles differ. Kolam in the south is drawn with rice flour as lines looping round a grid of dots, at dawn, on a swept and dampened floor. Wikipedia notes that coarse flour was used so ants and birds could feed on it. Alpana in Bengal is drawn freehand with rice-flour paste, often with lotuses, a granary or an owl linked to Lakshmi. In Kerala, flower carpets are laid for Onam and grow more complex over the ten days.

Rangoli is made for daily welcome and for festivals such as Diwali, Pongal, Onam, Durga Puja and weddings. It is often said to invite the goddess Lakshmi into the home. Several of these explanations are only weakly sourced, so they are best read as beliefs of the practice, not as proven history.
artist: Rangoli has no single named master. It is a household art, and sources say it is made traditionally by girls and women, with designs passed from one generation to the next. Men and boys also make it.

In Tamil Nadu, the month of Margazhi was a time when young women showed their skill with large kolams, sometimes covering a whole street. In Bengal, alpana is tied to bratas, religious fasts kept by women, and it is taught today at Kala Bhavana, the fine arts faculty of Visva-Bharati University.
Because the art is made fresh and then walked over or washed away, it lives in people's memory and hands more than in museums.
place: Rangoli belongs to the whole subcontinent, not to one place. The sources I read describe southern kolam as tidy and symmetric, and northern rangoli as more colourful and free.

Each region links the art to its own festival. Kolam and muggu go with the Pongal and Margazhi season in the south. Alpana goes with Durga Puja and Kali Puja in Bengal. In Odisha, designs called muruja and jhoti are made, and Wikipedia says they are often dedicated to Krishna and Jagannath. In Kerala, pookkalam belongs to Onam.
The map pins mark a few cities where particular styles are well known. They are examples, not boundaries.

history.what: The Sanskrit word ranga (colour) gives the name. Wikipedia says rangoli is mentioned in Hindu literature, but its claim about the Ramayana is marked as needing a source.
Wikipedia says the southern floor-drawing culture developed in the Chola era. I did not find a firmer source for this.
The month of Margazhi becomes known as a season for large kolams, linked in Sri Vaishnava tradition to the poet-saint Andal.
The earliest source cited by Wikipedia is a Bombay Presidency gazetteer of 1884.
Alpana is taken into art teaching at Visva-Bharati University.
Paint, stickers and coloured powders sit beside rice flour. Wikipedia reports that coloured-sand rangoli products were recalled in Australia and New Zealand over possible asbestos contamination.

future: Training: the art is still taught at home. Schools, festivals and competitions help children learn the regional patterns.
Livelihood: professional rangoli artists work at weddings and events. Their income is irregular and seasonal.
Materials: rice flour and flower petals are safe and cheap. Buyers should check coloured powders and sand, given the recall reported above.
Documentation: patterns and names vary by village. Recording them by region, with the women who know them, would help.
Protection: I found no GI or UNESCO listing for rangoli as a whole. Its best protection is daily use.

name: Rogan Art
tagline: Thick castor-oil paint drawn into patterns on cloth with a needle that never touches it.
facts: Form: paste painting on cloth with castor-oil colour
Kept alive by the Khatri family of Nirona, Kutch
Nirona Rogan art holds GI number 718, per the family's website
Rogan means oil in Persian
art: Rogan is a cloth painting made from a thick paste of boiled castor oil and colour. The Better India says the oil is heated and stirred for over 12 hours, then mixed with cold water into a sticky, elastic paste and combined with natural colours. It is stored in earthen pots.

The painter sits on the floor and draws the paste out with a blunt needle or rod, so that the tool does not touch the cloth. Often only half the design is drawn. The cloth is then folded to print the other half as a mirror image.
Common motifs are geometric flowers, peacocks and the tree of life. The finished cloth becomes wall hangings, saris, cushion covers and other items.
artist: The craft is held by the Khatri family of Nirona. Abdul Gafur Khatri has a State Award (1988), a National Award (1997) and the Padma Shri (2019), according to the family's website. The family says it is the only authentic family preserving the art.

The Better India says the art was passed down only through male members. The family's website says that since 2010 it has trained more than 400 girls, mostly from Nirona and Bhuj, and names Shahenajbanu Sumar Khatri as the first woman in the family to give live demonstrations. His younger brother Sumar Khatri and son Suleman Khatri are also named.
In 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi gave a rogan Tree of Life painting to US President Barack Obama, as reported by both sources. The family says it also has work at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
place: Nirona is a village in Kutch district, west Gujarat, north-west of Bhuj. The land is dry, but castor is grown locally and the artists buy the seed from nearby farmers.
Visitors can see the family at work in Nirona, where demonstrations and workshops are offered, according to the family's website.

history.what: The family's website says rogan came from Persia to Kutch about 400 years ago. The Better India says the Khatri family has practised it for over three centuries.
It decorated bridal trousseaus.
A secondary source says machine-made cloth hurt the craft. We could not check this in a primary source.
State and National awards go to Abdul Gafur Khatri.
The family begins training girls and women.
A rogan painting is gifted to President Obama.
Abdul Gafur Khatri receives the Padma Shri.

future: Training: keep opening classes to girls and to families outside the Khatris, as the family has begun to do.
Livelihood: build steady markets beyond gifts and fairs, since the Better India notes the family has struggled to earn from the craft.
Materials: secure castor oil from local farmers and safe natural colours.
Documentation: record the paste-making and drawing steps.
Protection: the family's site cites GI 718 for Nirona Rogan art; confirm in the registry.

name: Saura Paintings
tagline: Ritual wall paintings of the Saura, made to house a spirit.
facts: Also called idital or ikon
Made on house walls over red or yellow earth
Painted with brushes of bamboo twig
Often compared with Warli, but differs in its border
art: Saura paintings, called idital or ikon, are ritual wall paintings made by the Saura people of southern Odisha. They are painted for the gods and ancestors, not as decoration.

Wikipedia says the wall is prepared with red or yellow ochre earth, and the paint is white from ground stone and other natural colours, applied with brushes of bamboo shoot. OdishaBytes says the wall is made ready by women of the family, who also prepare a rice paste. Motifs include the sun, moon, axe, bow and arrow, elephant, horse, monkey, peacock and snake. Newer pictures show aeroplanes and bicycles.

Every idital has a detailed border. Human figures are drawn with smooth lines and the sexes are not easily told apart. Outlook Traveller says this sets it apart from Warli art, which has no marked border.
artist: OdishaBytes describes the specialist painter as the Idimar. Wikipedia says the priestly Kudang traditionally painted the ikons and explained them. The two names may refer to different roles or places, and the sources do not settle this.

According to OdishaBytes, a painting is called for when someone is ill for a long time. A shaman finds the spirit, and if it asks for a home, the family calls the Idimar. The painting takes up to three days, and the Idimar eats only after sunset in that time.
Verrier Elwin was the first outside scholar to study these paintings, says Wikipedia.
place: The Saura live mainly in Rayagada, Gajapati and Koraput, and also in Ganjam. OdishaBytes says the Lanjia, Jara, Arsi, Bhima and Sudha groups still keep the tradition, among 14 Saora subgroups.
OdishaBytes says the idital is placed in a dark corner of the house and is treated as the deities' house, responsible for family well-being.

history.what: Verrier Elwin, an anthropologist, is named as the first outsider to study the Saura pictographs.
OdishaBytes says the practice has nearly died out in places, due to modern culture and objections to animal sacrifice, which is part of the ritual.
The motifs have spread to canvas, paper, T-shirts and hotel walls. Wikipedia and OdishaBytes both note this commercial turn.

future: Livelihood: sell paintings on paper and cloth with the artist's name and village, so the income reaches the community.
Training: let young Saura learn from Idimars, with the community deciding what is public and what is ritual.
Materials: keep natural pigments and bamboo brushes in use.
Documentation: record meanings of each ikon with the painters' consent.
Protection: respect the sacred role of the work, and avoid copying it without the community.

name: Sohrai and Khovar Painting
tagline: Mud-wall murals by village women, cut into white clay with a comb.
facts: Form: wall murals made by women
Sohrai: harvest season; Khovar: marriage season
Four earth colours: black, white, red, yellow
Registered with a GI tag (sources give 2019 or 2020)
art: Sohrai and Khovar are mural traditions of the villages around Hazaribagh in Jharkhand. They are painted on the mud walls of houses by women. Sahapedia notes that the two names are broad umbrella terms for a range of practices, not single fixed styles.

Sohrai is painted in the harvest season, between about October and January, around the Sohrai festival that follows Diwali. Houses are repainted as a renewal that closes one farming year and opens the next. Khovar is painted for weddings. Its name is explained as kho (cave or shelter) and var (the bridal couple), so it refers to the decorated bridal room.

The colours come from local earth. Memeraki describes black from soil at field edges near forests, yellow from the clay potters also use, red from geru, and white from lime or kaolin pits. In the comb-cut method, a dark base is covered with white clay and the design is scratched out of the wet layer with a broken comb, fingers or twigs. Chewed neem twigs, cloth swabs and stencils are also used.

Common motifs are animals such as cattle, tigers, boar and nilgai, trees, lotus forests, lines and dots. Sources link the Sohrai animals to the painted rock shelters near Isko. Sahapedia says the Hazaribagh motifs include the tree of life and Pashupati. Designs and techniques differ from village to village.
artist: Women are the artists. Sahapedia names Kurmi women as the main painters around Hazaribagh, and says related wall painting is done by Adivasi and non-Adivasi women in Singhbhum. Men sometimes help by fetching clays.
A mural can take from a week to a month. Women fit it around household and farm work, and the monsoon limits when it can be done. Skills pass from mother to daughter.
The sources we could open name few individual painters. Memeraki names one Sohrai artist, Rukmani, in a photo caption. We have not named others we could not verify.
place: Hazaribagh lies on the northern Chota Nagpur plateau in Jharkhand. Memeraki contrasts hill villages with plains villages, which paint in somewhat different ways.

Painted rock shelters near Isko, in the Hazaribagh area, were brought to wider notice in the early 1990s by Bulu Imam of INTACH. Researchers have noted resemblances between their motifs and Sohrai and Khovar. How direct the link is remains a scholarly question.

history.what: Rock art at Isko, dated by researchers to a period between the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic, is compared with the modern murals. Sources describe the link as a resemblance of motifs, not proven descent.
Bulu Imam of INTACH Hazaribagh is credited by one source with first bringing the painted shelters to light.
Memeraki says a grant allowed INTACH to bring Sohrai designs onto paper, leading to exhibitions abroad.
Sahapedia says Bulu Imam and family founded the Tribal Women Artists Cooperative to revive the tradition.
Memeraki gives this as the year the Virasat Trust was founded; Sahapedia credits Justin Imam and Alka with the Virasat Foundation.
Sohrai Khovar painting received a Geographical Indication tag. Sources give 2019 and 2020; check the GI registry.
Sahapedia reports a fall in mural making, linked to less time, fewer mud houses and housing schemes that require brick and concrete.

future: Support women painters to keep painting their own walls as well as paper, as Virasat encourages.
Offer fair prices and direct sales for paper and cloth work, through the women's cooperative that holds the GI.
Help families who move to brick houses keep a wall or panel for Sohrai and Khovar.
Record each village's patterns and techniques, with the women as the named authors.
Protect the clay and lime sources that supply the four colours, and teach girls the colour-making.

name: Talapatra (Palm-Leaf Manuscripts)
tagline: Scenes scratched into dried palm leaf with an iron stylus.
facts: Also called tala patta chitra
Tool: an iron stylus
Main centre: Raghurajpur, near Puri
Leaves are dried, soaked and treated with turmeric
art: Talapatra, also called tala patta chitra, is the art of engraving on palm leaf. The line is scratched into the leaf with a pointed iron stylus. Colour is then rubbed over the surface with a cloth so that it settles in the cut lines.

Indian Villez describes the preparation. Leaves are dried for a month or two, soaked in water and cut to size. A turmeric solution is applied for longevity. Colours are made by the artists from sources such as conch shell, lamp soot and green leaves. A slip of the stylus cannot be undone, as palm leaves are fragile.
Subjects are mostly religious and mythological: the Gita Govinda, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and devotion to Lord Jagannath. Skilled hands also decorate cards, lamp shades and other objects.
artist: The article names Benudhar Mohapatra as a master who trained many artists and won awards, and his son Arun U. Mohapatra as a state awardee. It speaks of about 500 artists in the area.
We could read only one detailed source on this craft, so this entry is short.
place: Raghurajpur is a small hamlet near Puri and is the main centre. Indian Villez also lists smaller centres at Nayakpatna, Balanga, Nikalata, Jatni, Balipatna and Kalapathar.
Indian Villez says Cyclone Fani in 2019 destroyed many paintings.

history.what: Indian Villez says the art began around the 5th century BCE and was first used for horoscopes and manuscripts. It also mentions an unclear, much longer journey of the art, so we treat the early dates as uncertain.
It grew from writing and manuscript illustration into an independent art, and it is now applied to decorative goods.
Cyclone Fani damaged paintings and stocks in the area.

future: Livelihood: widen the market through craft fairs and online sales, as the source notes the market is shrinking.
Training: keep master-and-student teaching alive in Raghurajpur.
Materials: a steady supply of well-seasoned palm leaf and natural colours.
Documentation: record old manuscripts and the stories the leaves carry.
Protection: Indian Villez says a GI tag is being sought for legal protection.

name: Thangka
tagline: A mountain monastery you can roll up and carry.
facts: Medium: cotton or silk scroll
Pigments: mineral and plant colours, gold
Subject: Buddhas, mandalas, the Wheel of Life
art: A thangka is a Buddhist painting on cloth, framed in silk brocade, that can be rolled up and carried. It depicts the Buddha, bodhisattvas, protector deities and mandalas.
The proportions of every figure follow strict iconographic rules, and the image is a support for meditation as well as art.
artist: Thangka painting is a long apprenticeship, in monasteries and art schools, often lasting years, under a master.
Artists begin with sacred measurements and a ritual before painting.
Our approach: honour the lineage and the teacher behind each painter.
place: Sikkim and Ladakh are Himalayan Buddhist regions. Gangtok has institutions devoted to Tibetan studies, and the region has monasteries such as Rumtek. Leh lies on the Indus in high-altitude desert, with monasteries on the hills nearby.
In these places Buddhism, mountain climate and trade routes shaped art over centuries.

history.what: The art travelled with Buddhism across the Himalaya and Tibet.
Tibetan refugees brought teachers and styles to India, strengthening the art.
Both traditional temple thangkas and modern works are made.

future: Care for mountain monastery collections through shared conservation.
Apprenticeship paths for local young people.
Respectful display: sacred images presented with context.

images.alt: A thangka painting of a Buddhist teacher with attendant figures.
images.author: Paintings on clothes in a cloth shop at Miao, Arunachal Pradesh. Photographer: D

name: Thanjavur Painting
tagline: Gold, gems and devotion on a wooden panel.
facts: Medium: wood panel with cloth
Materials: gesso relief, gold leaf, semi-precious stones
Subject: Hindu deities and saints
art: Thanjavur (Tanjore) paintings glow. Figures of Krishna, Ganesha, Lakshmi and Rama sit centred in an arch or throne, in rich colours, with raised gesso work covered in gold foil and sometimes set with glass or stones.
The base is a wooden plank covered with cloth; the drawing is laid in first, then the relief, then gold leaf and colour.
artist: The craft has been practised by families such as the Naidus and Rajus. Painters from Thanjavur and nearby Tiruchirappalli also made smaller works.
Women and men both paint today, and many artists have trained in local workshops or art schools.
Our approach: show the layers of an artwork being built, step by step, with the artist narrating.
place: Thanjavur lies in the Kaveri delta, the 'rice bowl of Tamil Nadu', and is the seat of the Chola-era Brihadisvara temple and the Tamil classical music and Bharatanatyam traditions.
The region's temples, courts and festivals have long been the art's patrons.

history.what: Painting traditions flourished in southern temples.
The Maratha rulers of Thanjavur patronised the style that became known as Thanjavur painting.
British officers and travellers bought the works as souvenirs.
The craft has a geographical-indication status and is made for homes and temples.

future: Fair gold: promote gold-foil use in sustainable amounts and transparency in materials.
Teach the technique to young artists through short residencies.
Connect with music and dance: pair paintings with the delta's music and Bharatanatyam stories.

images.alt: A Thanjavur painting of Krishna and Radha on a swing, with gold foil.

name: Tikuli Art
tagline: The bindi turned into a painting: once glass and gold foil, now enamel on hardboard.
facts: Tikuli is the local word for the bindi
Said to be about 800 years old; dates are not firm
Revived by Upendra Maharathi, from 1954 by most accounts
Now painted in enamel on hardboard
art: Tikuli began as the forehead ornament. Gaon Connection describes the older method: molten glass cut into small round pieces, covered with gold foil, with designs traced in with a sharp bamboo tool, coloured, and sealed with gond, a natural gum.

The modern craft moved to hardboard. The Better India says artists cut the board into circles, rectangles and other shapes, apply four or five coats of enamel and sand between coats, then paint the design and add gold foil. Brushes are fine, made of squirrel or sable hair. Dry weather suits the enamel.
Designs often use Madhubani motifs, and the common themes are Krishna Leela, weddings and Bihar festivals. Products include wall pieces, coasters, trays and pen stands.
artist: Upendra Maharathi (1908-1981) is the central name. Sources say he saw enamel on wood being used in Japan and brought the idea back. Gaon Connection and The Better India date this to 1954, while another source says 1950. The Better India calls him Padmashree Upendra Maharathi.

Ashok Kumar Biswas and his wife Shibani Biswas carried the revival forward. Gaon Connection says Biswas has trained hundreds of women and received the Guru Shishya Parampara award in 2022. Women from rural areas, such as Arti Devi and Sapna Kumari quoted in that article, now earn from the craft.
Gaon Connection also notes that Muslim artisans once cut the glass and Hindu artists applied the gold, a shared effort.
place: Patna, on the Ganga, is the home of Tikuli. Gaon Connection says Patna, Varanasi and Kolkata are the main hubs for buying and selling. Biswas's training centre is described as being near Patna.
Patna was a trading city under the Mughals, and the sources link the craft's best days to that period.

history.what: Sources say Tikuli began in the Patna region. Biswas, quoted by Gaon Connection, links it to Mauryan-era ornaments. These two dates do not match, and no source proves either.
The craft is said to have flourished with royal and aristocratic patrons.
Cheap machine-made bindis replaced the handmade ones and many artisans lost work, per The Better India.
Upendra Maharathi moves the craft to enamel on wood, per two sources. One source says 1950.
Gaon Connection says this was the last year government bought artwork directly from artists.
Gaon Connection mentions a state policy to promote Tikuli training.

future: Training: more centres for women, with paid learning time
Livelihood: direct buyers and a government market, since artisans say state buying stopped in 1984
Materials: enamel and hardboard are cheap, so keep options open, including a small line of traditional glass and gold work
Documentation: record the glass-and-gold method while older artisans remember it
Protection: seek GI or similar recognition, if the community wants it

name: Usta Art (Bikaner)
tagline: Gold laid over raised paint on camel hide, by the Usta families of Bikaner.
facts: Forms: manoti (embossed gold) and naqqashi (flat gold)
GI tag for Bikaner Usta Kala: August 2023
Fewer than 70 artists practise it today
Hisam-ud-din Usta (1910-1987) received the Padma Shri in 1986
art: Usta art is the work of the Usta artisans of Bikaner. Wikipedia describes two main forms. Manoti is embossed, with gold layered over painted floral patterns. Naqqashi uses the same methods but with flat, unembossed gold.

Wikipedia lists the steps: priming the surface, drawing the design, painting floral motifs, embossing with a paste, adding yellow layers, and laying gold foil with fine detailing. The work decorates walls, ceilings, glass, wood and marble as well as camel-hide objects.
Camel-hide pots, once used for oil and fragrance, became a portable surface, and Wikipedia ties this to the period of British rule.
artist: Hisam-ud-din Usta (1910-1987) is described by Wikipedia as the last formally trained painter in the Bikaner school style. He won a national award in 1967 and the Padma Shri in 1986.
101 Reporters says that by 1967 he was the only artist left, and that efforts in 1976 led to a Camel Hide Training Centre and to students taking up the art.

The same report says fewer than 70 artists work today. A piece can take months, and mastery takes three to five years. Artists say short government training camps are not enough, and few women take part. Pieces sell from about Rs 7,000 to Rs 50,000.
place: Bikaner is in the Thar desert region of north-west Rajasthan. Usta work can still be seen in the Anup, Phool and Karan Mahals of Junagarh Fort, according to Wikipedia.
NIFT Jodhpur and the USTTAD scheme have supported artists, per 101 Reporters.

history.what: Wikipedia says Usta artists came to Bikaner under Maharaja Rai Singh in Akbar's time to decorate Junagarh Fort. 101 Reporters says Rai Singh invited artists from Iran. Other sources give other stories, so treat these as tradition.
Camel-hide objects spread as portable pieces, according to Wikipedia.
Hisam-ud-din Usta receives a national award for master craftspeople. By this year he was the only remaining artist, per 101 Reporters.
A training centre and new students revive the art, per 101 Reporters.
Padma Shri to Hisam-ud-din Usta.
Bikaner Usta Kala receives a GI tag, per 101 Reporters.

future: Offer longer courses than two or three months.
Open the craft to women and to people outside the Usta families.
Use the GI tag with artist names on each work, as planned.
Create schemes made for this craft and tell artists about them.
Document Bikaner's palace murals as a record to learn from.

name: Warli
tagline: A whole world drawn from a circle, a triangle and a line.
facts: Medium: mud walls, now cloth and paper
Pigment: white rice paste on red-ochre ground
Tools: bamboo stick brush
art: Warli paintings use only a few shapes: the circle for the sun and moon, the triangle for mountains and trees, the square for sacred enclosures. Human figures are two triangles joined at the tip, and the picture tells everyday life: harvests, dances, hunting, fishing.
The central ritual image is the chowk, drawn for weddings, built around Palaghata, the goddess of fertility. A circular spiral of dancers, the tarpa dance, often fills the frame.
artist: Warli art was traditionally made by women, often the suvasini (married women) during weddings. Men were not usually the painters.

Jivya Soma Mashe, from Kalambipada in Dahanu, is widely credited with taking the art beyond ritual in the 1970s, painting daily life as an end in itself. He received a Padma Shri in 2011. His sons and others continue his work.
Our approach: record artists in their own words, in Warli and Marathi, with translation.
place: The Warli are an adivasi community living in the hills and coast of Palghar and parts of Thane in northern Maharashtra, as well as adjoining Gujarat. Their villages sit between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea.
The nearness of Mumbai means the same land has seen rapid change: farms, brick kilns and commuter towns are close together.

history.what: Scholars connect the drawing style with ancient rock art shapes, though dating is debated. Walls were painted fresh for each ritual.
Jivya Soma Mashe began painting on paper and cloth and exhibiting; the art gained a national audience.
Government and NGO programmes encouraged Warli painters to produce for the market.
Warli motifs appear on textiles, home decor and public walls, sometimes copied without credit to the community.
